en: The *Vīryavegarāja-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, Volume One, translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Bhagavān was dwelling in the city of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove.

In the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, he was together with a great assembly of twenty thousand bhikṣus and ten thousand bodhisattva-mahāsattvas, headed by Maitreya Bodhisattva, Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva, Siṃhamati Bodhisattva, Siṃhadhvaja Bodhisattva, Mahādhvaja Bodhisattva, and others, all of whom were destined to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi in their final birth.
At that time, there was among the assembly a bodhisattva mahāsattva named Veṣṭhitarāja, seated within the great gathering.

At that moment, the World-Honored One was surrounded by hundreds of thousands of immeasurable attendants who paid him respectful homage and made offerings as he preached the Dharma—that which is practiced by those of the Mahāyāna.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Veṣṭhitarāja rose from his seat, adjusted his robes, placed his right shoulder and right knee upon the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, prostrated with his head at the Buddha’s feet, and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One!”
"I now wish to ask the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, about a certain teaching; I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain it for me.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vegeśvara, saying: "Vegeśvara!"
"Ask whatever you wish, and I shall explain it for you. O Veṣṭhita-rāja!
If you ask, then according to your own intention and whatever you inquire about, I shall explain it to you in such a way as to bring joy to your heart."
The Bodhisattva Veṣṭhitarāja said:
“So it is, World-Honored One!
I wish and desire to hear it.”
Having received permission, the Bodhisattva Veṣṭhitarāja was filled with great joy and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
what is the Great Vehicle’s display of power (*vega*) of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas?”

Furthermore, for the sake of sentient beings, you preach this Mahāyāna, whereby—through that heroic prowess—you shatter all Māras, all arrogant persons, all disputants, and all those who delight in views based on conceptual discrimination, causing them to abide in the Mahāyāna, fulfill their great vows, achieve perfection in ethical conduct, and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vegeśvara, saying:
“Excellent, excellent, Vegeśvara!”
Excellent, O Vigourous King!
You have now skillfully questioned the Tathāgata regarding such a meaning; you should keep this well in mind.

Listen attentively, listen attentively, O Vigourous King, and reflect upon it well. I shall now analyze and explain for you the vigor of a bodhisattva and the Great Vehicle, and further explain this Great Vehicle for the sake of sentient beings, so that by means of that vigor they may destroy all Māras, all arrogant people, and all those who delight in views based on conceptual discrimination, causing them to abide in the Great Vehicle, fulfill their great vows, achieve the perfection of ethical conduct, and attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Bodhisattva Veṣṭhita-rāja said:
“So it is, World-Honored One!
I wish and desire to hear it.”
The Buddha addressed the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Vegeśvara, saying:
“Vegeśvara, there are four kinds of vege (vega).”
What are these four?
First, the valor of ethical discipline; second, the valor of supernormal powers; third, the valor of knowledge; and fourth, the valor of wisdom.
"Vīryendrarāja!
These are the four kinds of *vega* of a bodhisattva. Vīryendrarāja!"
What is the "mastery of ethical discipline" (*śīla-vidhūta*)?
It is the perfection of ethical discipline by this bodhisattva, namely:

ethical discipline that is unimpaired, ethical discipline that is unpierced, ethical discipline that is unmixed, ethical discipline that is undifferentiated, and ethical discipline that is free from regret.
The precept of non-destruction, the precept of non-feverishness, the precept of excellent protection, the precept praised by the wise, the precept conforming to the Path,
the precept of accomplishing the dharmas of others, the precept of protecting all dharmas, the precept of joyful affection,
the precept of not relying on birth within any realm of existence, the precept of abiding in *śamatha*, and the precept of conforming to *vipaśyanā*.
The precept of liberation through the profound Dharma; the precept of non-retrogressive supernormal powers; the precept of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; the precept of pure tranquility;
the precept of proclaiming the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; the precept of not abandoning any sentient being;
the precept of the mind that protects with loving-kindness; the precept rooted in great compassion; the precept of pure faith; and the precept of non-discriminatory deportment.
The precepts of the dhūta virtues; the precepts of the field of merit; the precepts of ultimate purity;

the precepts that do not sever the lineage of the Tathāgata; the precepts that protect the lineage of the Dharma; the precepts of beholding the noble Saṃgha; the precepts of abiding well in the bodhicitta;

the precepts of abiding in the six pāramitās; and the precepts for the cultivation of the foundations of mindfulness, right efforts, bases of power, faculties, powers, and the factors of enlightenment.
The precepts of the Eightfold Noble Path; the precepts that give rise to all factors conducive to enlightenment.
"Vikrāntarāja! When a bodhisattva is thus fully endowed with these precepts, their great vows are accomplished."
What is that vow?
When the kalpa has ended and is being consumed by fire, and flames fill the trichiliocosm, a bodhisattva who is fully endowed with the precepts makes this vow:
"May this be great, profound quiescence."
The fire was immediately extinguished.
If he wished to fill this trichiliocosm with water, the water would immediately fill it;
if he wished to fill it with flowers, they would immediately fill it according to his will.
If he wishes to fill it with jewels, all manner of precious gems immediately fill it;
furthermore, if he wishes to make all the Sumeru Kings of Mounts in worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges into a single mountain, they immediately become one mountain.

Vīryaketu! When a bodhisattva has thus become fully endowed with ethical discipline, if he wishes to cause all the great oceans within as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges to become a single ocean, they immediately become a single ocean.

Abiding in the power of ethical discipline (*śīla-bala*), all that they wish for according to their hearts' desires is fully accomplished; there is nothing among their thoughts that is not fulfilled as they intend.
"Vikrāntarāja! It is in this way that a bodhisattva abiding in ethical discipline manifests such prowess."
"If a person abides in the precepts, their vows will be fulfilled, namely, *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

'Vikrāntagāmin, in the remote past, beyond incalculable upon incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas— in immeasurable, inconceivable great kalpas— there appeared in the world a Buddha named Prabhāsa-vimalaprabhārāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, Vidya-caraṇa-saṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddha, Bhagavān.'"

“Vīryendrarāja! At that time, within the Dharma of the Tathāgata Vimalaprabhāsa-rāja, there was a bodhisattva named Vajrānta, who dwelt securely in the power of ethical discipline and whose precepts were perfectly pure.”
In that Vajra-Row hermitage, he practiced walking meditation with diligence, delighting in the cultivation of the noble Dharma and desiring to fulfill the Buddha-dharma.
He, Vajra-Row, observed thus:
"If one does not differentiate any phenomena, this is what is called precept."
If one does not take delight in any things, it is then called precept;
if one can extinguish all afflictions, it is then called precept;
if one knows that the body and its reflected image are equal, it is then called precept.
If one regards speech and echoes as equal, it is called precept;
if one contemplates mental phenomena as being like illusions and without distinction, it is called precept;
if one sees that the two dharmas of good and non-good are non-dual, it is called precept.
If one eliminates and extinguishes lust through the contemplation of impurity, it is then called precept;
if one eliminates and extinguishes hatred and anger through the contemplation of loving-kindness and compassion, it is then called precept;
if one eliminates and extinguishes delusion through wisdom, it is then called precept.
If one does not discriminate between greed, hatred, and delusion, it is called precept;
if one discriminates that all phenomena are non-discriminatory, it is called precept;
if there is no view of self, no view of a sentient being, no view of a life-force, no view of a person, and no view of permanence, it is called precept.
If all phenomena are practiced without attachment, it is called precept;
if one is not terrified by any state of mind, it is called precept;
if the mind does not rely upon the three realms, it is called precept.
If one has faith that all phenomena are entirely non-arising, it may be called precept;
if the mind believes in and understands the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas, it may be called precept;
if one does not crave wealth, profit, or offerings, it may be called precept.
If one does not fear emptiness, it is only then called precept;
if one cultivates signlessness, it is only then called precept;
if one is free from seeking and wishing, it is only then called precept.
If one does not grasp at the precepts within the aggregate of ethical discipline, it may be called true discipline;
if one does not exalt oneself or disparage others on account of maintaining the aggregate of precepts, it may be called true discipline;
if one does not praise the sense bases (*āyatana*), it may be called true discipline.
If one does not act upon nor become attached to sense objects, it is then called precept;
if one is equanimous toward the five aggregates and the aggregate of phenomena (dharmaskandha), it is then called precept;
if one is equanimous toward the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) within the [eighteen] realms, it is then called precept.
If one does not engage in disputes, it is then called precept;
if one does not cease from all wholesome dharmas, it is then called precept;
if one ultimately knows that all dharmas are entirely quiescent, and having known this quiescence, the body then acts correctly, it is then called precept.
“Vīryaketu-rāja!

At that time, the Bodhisattva Vajrāntā established himself in the perfection of ethical discipline through such dharmas; he practiced the noble Dharma, applied himself with diligent vigor, and did not depart from right contemplation.”

A son of Māra named Cchā, seeing that bhikṣu abiding in the perfection of precepts through such dharmas, practicing the noble Dharma, exerting himself with diligence, and never departing from right contemplation as he practiced walking meditation, led a host of eighty-four thousand troops—all clad in armor yet concealing their own bodies—to the bhikṣu’s location to seek an opportunity against him, following the bhikṣu for a thousand years.
Thus, for a thousand years, that Māra could not find even a single moment of distracted mind in that bhikṣu.
Seeking such mental distraction, Māra would have provided obstacles, terrors, and disturbances had he found it.

At that time, Cāmara and his host sought an opportunity for a thousand years without success; they then manifested themselves again, all grasping swords, spears, and various weapons, appearing before the bhikṣu to intimidate him and cause him fear.
When the bodhisattva bhikṣu Vajrānta saw the hosts of Māra’s army holding various weapons such as swords and spears, and having been terrified by them, he immediately made this vow:
“I now truly, within this Dharma, practice the cultivation of the pure aggregate of precepts through right contemplation.”

If this matter is indeed true, may the various weapons held in the hands of the māra followers—swords, spears, and all manner of armaments—all be transformed into various flower garlands: *utpala*, *padma*, *kumuda*, *puṇḍarīka*, *campaka*, *sumana*, and *vārṣika* flowers;
and may all these celestial māra bodies and their military hosts assume my own form and maintain my very same majestic deportment.

"Vikrāntarāja! Once the bhikṣu Bodhisattva Vajrācchā has made this vow, all the swords, spears, and various weapons held by the entire host of Māras immediately transform into various exquisite flowers, of immeasurable colors and variegated hues, possessing a sublime fragrance that delights the mind upon being seen or smelled; they are exceptionally pleasing and wonderful.

The physical appearance, forms, and attire of all the Māras become identical to those of the bhikṣu; they all appear as if they have gone forth—wearing the *kāṣāya* robes and having shaved their hair and beards—visible to both themselves and others."

“Vīryendrarāja! At that time, when Cchama saw the monk’s superior supernatural powers, he was struck with wonder; together with his host of armies, he prostrated at the feet of that monk, Vajrānta, and asked:
‘Great Sage!’”
"What dharma have you attained that you are able to abide in such supernormal power? "O King Vikrama!
At that time, the bodhisattva bhikṣu Vajrānta replied to Cchama:"
"Great Seer, you should know:
such dharmas do not abide by way of existence, because all dharmas are unattainable.
Great Seer, you should know:"
Body, speech, and mind are all without dependence; this lack of dependence is my dwelling, for all phenomena abide without dependence.
Great Seer, you should know that one who dwells in this manner does not dwell in the mark of existence, nor does he dwell in the mark of non-existence; such is called "dwelling."
"One who dwells in this manner does not dwell in any existent phenomenon; because there is no dwelling and no location, it is called 'dwelling.
At that time, Cāmara addressed the Bodhisattva Bhikṣu Vajrasamudgata, saying:
"For a thousand years I have observed your mental conduct, constantly seeking an opportunity against you, yet I have been unable to find one."
Then the Bodhisattva Bhikṣu Vajrānta said: “Great Seer!
Even if you were to seek the movement of my mind for as many eons as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River, you would still be unable to find it.”
Why is this? Because the mind is not within, nor is it without; it is not in both places together, nor is it in between.
Furthermore, O Great Sage!
“Have you not perceived the mental activities of the illusory person?
The Māra replied, “Bhikṣu! [I have.]”
"It cannot be found.
As for that illusory person, they have no mind and no thought; where could they be found?
The Bodhisattva Bhikṣu replied:
“Great Seer!
The Tathāgata has always said:
‘All dharmas are like illusory appearances; no mind can be apprehended, and no thought can be apprehended.’”
The Māra said:
"Bhikṣu! If you have no mind and no thought that can be apprehended, how do you act?"
"Does it go or does it come?
Furthermore, how can there be any speech?
The Bodhisattva Bhikṣu replied:
"O Great Sage!
Just as a person created by illusion moves about, comes, goes, and speaks;
so do I move, come, go, and speak."
The Māra said:

"Bhikṣu! If it is as you say, and you thus exert yourself with diligence, abide securely in the observance of the precepts, and practice the noble Dharma—what is it that you seek by undertaking such an endeavor?"
The bhikṣu replied:
“There is no arousal, no practice, and no place for seeking. Māra said:
"What is meant by 'no setting forth, no practice, and no place of seeking'?
The bhikṣu replied, "In such a state,
there is no person who goes, no person who comes, and no person who shall go."
Great Seer, you should know:
that which is without arousal and without activity is called wishlessness.
Furthermore, Great Seer!
If you should ask:
"You exert yourself with diligence, abide securely in the observance of the precepts, and practice the noble Dharma; what do you seek by undertaking such an endeavor?"
"Regarding those who ask such questions, you should now listen:
This seeking of mine does not seek the arising of form, nor the cessation of form, nor the location of form.

Likewise, it does not seek the arising of feeling, perception, volitional formations, or consciousness; nor does it seek the cessation of consciousness, nor the location of consciousness. This extends to all phenomena as well—it neither seeks their arising, nor their cessation, nor their location."
Great Seer, you should know this:

if that true state is not comprised within form, and likewise is not comprised within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—this is the place I seek; if that place I seek cannot be seen, it is the place I seek.

If that right sphere were not comprised within form, and likewise were not comprised within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness—if such a right sphere were the place where I seek, yet I do not perceive that place where I seek—then [it would be so].
"Great Seer, you should know:
I seek in the same manner as the Noble Ones seek. Māra said:
“Bhikṣu! How does one seek that state of the noble ones?
The Bodhisattva Bhikṣu replied:
"O Great Sage!
Whether they be the dharmas of ordinary beings or the dharmas of the Buddhas, all these dharmas are equal and non-dual;
whether they be the dharmas of those in training, the dharmas of those beyond training, or the dharmas of the Buddhas, all these dharmas are equal and non-dual."
Whether it be the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas or the dharmas of the Buddhas, all these dharmas are equal and non-dual;
whether it be past dharmas, future dharmas, or present dharmas, all these dharmas are equal and non-dual.
It is equal because it is non-arising;
it is equal because it is non-emerging;
it is equal because it is non-ceasing.
If a person does not abandon such equanimity, they cultivate equanimity and are therefore able to preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
Great Seer, you should know:
I seek such a state of right abiding in this manner.
Great Seer, you should know this:
such a right state is not a place within the desire realm, nor a place within the form realm, nor a place within the formless realm.
If a person abides thus in equanimity, they are unmoving in accordance with the Dharma; they neither engage in practice nor refrain from it, and they do not cause others to practice.
Great Seer, you should know this:
it is called the "right station. Just as that [practice] is set forth, all dharmas are set forth in such a manner;
just as the dharma-realm is set forth, all dharmas are set forth in such a manner.
Just as the issue proceeds according to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), so do all phenomena proceed.
If one seeks in this manner, that person does not perceive a place of activity and the mind finds no delight; therefore, it is called the "right place" (*samyak-sthāna*).
At that time, Cchama addressed the Bodhisattva Bhikṣu Vajrasamudgata, saying these words:
"What is attained by this correct practice?"
The bhikṣu replied:
"In this right cultivation, I have attained non-attainment; there is no non-attainment, for it is equal and fully satisfied.
Furthermore, as for what you asked:"
Regarding the question, "What dharma is attained?"—if there is anything attained, it is not correct practice; because one is free from conceit, it is called correct practice.
One who practices correctly has no dharma to be attained; that which is called "correct practice" involves nothing to be practiced.
At that time, Cāmara asked the bhikṣu Vajrasaṃhati these words:
"For what purpose is this perfection of the precepts sought?"
The bhikṣu replied:
"I abide in this precept in order to seek anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, to realize the dharma that is non-extinguished, and to attain the dharma that is non-arising."
The Māra asked:
"What is it that is awakened to in bodhi?
The bhikṣu replied:
“The awakening to the equality of form is the awakening to bodhi; the awakening to the equality of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness is it;
the awakening to the equality of all dharmas is the awakening to bodhi.”
The Māra said:
"Bhikṣu! Where is that bodhi to be sought?"
He replied: "Great Seer!
That which is called 'awakening' (bodhi) is to be sought within the view of a self-identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi)."
Māra asked again, "How do you seek it?
The bhikṣu replied:
“Awakening does not arise from the view of a body, nor does it arise as one seeks the view of a body;
awakening is likewise, and thus do I seek it.
At that time, Cāmara asked the bhikṣu Vajrasama these words:
"Who is your teacher?
Who instructed you in such eloquence? He replied:
"O Great Sage!
He who attains bodhi without being angry with himself is my teacher;
he who dwells neither in defilement nor in purity is my teacher."
If there is a person whose consciousness dwells neither in permanence nor in impermanence, he is my teacher;
if someone comes to hear the Dharma from him—the Dharma that does not dwell and the Dharma that is non-conceptual—and having heard it thus, crosses the ocean of ignorance, he is my teacher;
if his wisdom is able to know all dharmas not through sequential knowledge, he is my teacher.
If one can thoroughly know all speech without sequential cognition and without conceptual differentiation, he is my teacher;
if one does not give rise to or produce any phenomena yet turns the wheel of the noble Dharma, he is my teacher;
if one abides neither there, nor here, nor in between, he is my teacher.
If one says that all phenomena are unborn yet arise of themselves, he is my teacher;
if one says that all phenomena are unceasing yet cease of themselves, he is my teacher.
"I have obtained such eloquence from that teacher. Māra said, "Bhikṣu!
"How does the Tathāgata turn the wheel of Dharma? The bhikṣu replied: "It is not the turning of form;

it is not the suchness of form; it is not the dharma of form; it is not the emptiness of form; it is not the signlessness of form; it is not the wishlessness of form; it is not the tranquility of form; it is not the detachment of form; it is not the non-arising of form; it is not the intrinsic nature of form; it is not the self-essence of form; it is not the turning of a self-essence; nor is it non-turning."
In this same sequence, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness neither turn nor do not turn.

Consciousness is according to the nature of consciousness: empty, signless, wishless, tranquil, detached, unborn, and its intrinsic nature is neither turning nor non-turning. The Dharma-wheel of the Tathāgata turns in this manner; all Dharma-wheels are thus turned.
Whether that wheel of Dharma turns or does not turn, the limit of fruition within the immeasurable dharma-realm is never abandoned;
if a person can know when that wheel of Dharma turns, for such a person the wheel indeed turns.
At that time, Cāmara and his host of armies took the Bodhisattva Bhikṣu Vajrasama as their disciple and spoke these words:
"Now we, this assembly, take refuge in you, O Virtuous One."
That bhikṣu said: “Do not take refuge in me;
you should take refuge in the Tathāgata King of Stainless Radiance. This Dharma that has been taught is the Buddha-dharma of that [Tathāgata].”
He said, "Come, let us go together to the place where the Tathāgata resides.
Then, the bodhisattva bhikṣu Vajrakaṭhika, together with the eight thousand four hundred māras led by Cāmara, went to the presence of the World-Honored One, the Buddha Prabhāsa-vimala-prabha-rāja.
Having arrived at the Buddha’s dwelling, they prostrated with their heads at his feet, joined their palms toward the Buddha, and stood to one side.
Then that Tathāgata, for the sake of that host of Māras, taught the sequence of abiding in the precepts up to the practice of the noble Dharma, speaking in accordance with the Dharma.
"In this way, all Māras do not regress from anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
O Vegeśvara, what do you think?"
Who else could that Bodhisattva Bhikṣu Vajrānta have been?
Do not view him as anyone other than this. Why is that?
"You yourself are that bhikṣu Vajrānta Bodhisattva, and the Bodhisattva Dharaṇīdhara is that Cchama.
O Vegeśvara, this is the bodhisattva’s *vega* of ethical discipline."

Once the Bodhisattva has attained this sovereign power of ethical discipline (*śīla-vaśitā*), inconceivable and supreme vows also manifest; he brings immeasurable sentient beings to maturity in bodhi, destroys the enmity of Māra, and swiftly attains the awakening of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
“Vīryendrarāja! What is the bodhisattva’s supernormal power of mastery (*abhijñāvikrīḍita*)?
Why is it called the supernormal power of mastery?”
“Vīryendrarāja!
There are five kinds of them. What are the five?
First, the divine eye; second, the divine ear; third, knowledge of others' minds; fourth, recollection of past lives; and fifth, supernormal powers.
"Vīryendrarāja! What is the Bodhisattva’s supernormal power of the divine eye?

If one possesses the faculty of the eye, it is not obstructed by walls; trees, forests, mountains, Mount Sumeru, the Cakravāḍa mountains, or any mountains within a world-system cannot act as obstructions."

With unobstructed eyes, he is able to see the infinite and incalculable Buddha-worlds of the ten directions as if they were a single world; where there are material objects, he perceives them as if they were empty space, such that these various worlds do not obstruct one another at all.

With an equal and singular vision, one beholds all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, in those Buddha-worlds, surrounded by their assemblies of śrāvakas; one sees every single Buddha. Because of the unimpeded cultivation of faith and understanding in a single Buddha, the entire dharma-realm is realized:
if one sees one Buddha, all Buddhas are seen as utterly pure;
if one sees all Buddhas, that one Buddha is seen as pure.
In this way, if one perceives the purity of the Buddha, one enters into purity for oneself;
if one thus enters into purity for oneself, then all phenomena are seen as pure. Seeing oneself as pure and seeing phenomena as pure, one does not grasp at these two characteristics.
If those Blessed Ones and the śrāvakas see, they see the purity of the Buddha; seeing the śrāvakas, they do not see anything different.
To see the śrāvakas is to see the Buddha; to see the Buddha is to see the śrāvakas.

“If all sentient beings within those immeasurable and boundless worlds—those comprised among sentient beings, whether in the bodies of hell-beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, devas, or asuras; whether acting in the desire realm, with the exception of those in the formless realm—all of them are seen, and he knows their karmic retributions, whether they are falling away, being born, decreasing, or increasing.”

They know and perceive sentient beings and they know the retribution of karma, yet they do not actually give rise to the notion of "sentient beings," because they know that all sentient beings are without self;
although they know the retribution of karma, they have no notion of "retribution of karma," for they have entered into the state where all phenomena are without retribution of karma.

"One should know that although that person with the divine eye sees all forms, they do not grasp at the characteristics of form. This is because all forms are without intrinsic substance, because the perception of the characteristics of all forms is unreal, and because the primordial limit of all forms is empty."
“By what causes and conditions can that person with the divine eye see in such a way?
It is by the power of wisdom that they are able to see in this manner.
Just as they see it, so do I see it; yet according to the desires of one's own mind, one may not see anything at all.”
If the mind desires to see all forms, it sees them immediately according to that intention; there is not even the slightest form that the eye does not see.
Yet, among immeasurable hundreds of thousands of sentient beings, that person may practice dhyāna, liberation, samādhi, and samāpatti, while those sentient beings do not see him with their eyes.
Why is this? It is because such a bodhisattva knows that, in accordance with *tathatā*, there is no self in phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).

That person desires—whether it be the subtle body, the excellent body, the radiant body, or the incomparable body of a deity in the realm of form—to manifest a bodhisattva’s body within that heaven so as to show it to the deity, enabling that deity to see the bodhisattva’s body; in this way, the bodhisattva likewise sees the body of that deity.
If he wishes to cause the devas to see the Bodhisattva’s body as well as their own bodies, they are immediately able to see them;
if he wishes to cause the devas to see only their own bodies and not the Bodhisattva, they immediately see themselves and do not see the Bodhisattva;
if he wishes to cause the devas to see the Bodhisattva’s body and not their own bodies, they immediately see the Bodhisattva and do not see their own bodies.
Vīryendriyarāja!
A bodhisattva accomplishes such divine sight.
Vīryendriyarāja!
What is the bodhisattva’s mastery of the supernormal power of the divine ear?

That bodhisattva achieves the divine ear and hears all sounds throughout immeasurable and boundless worlds—sounds of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans; he hears all such sounds.

Although they hear those sounds, they do not grasp at the characteristic of self or the characteristic of sentient beings; they do not grasp at the characteristic of sound, yet they know the characteristics of all vocal sounds.
Although they hear these sounds, they have faith and understanding that the locus of sound is unreal, for both preceding and succeeding sounds are entirely without sound.
Having realized this, that sound has no location; with the conviction that it has no location, the ear-faculty, consciousness, and element are then without obstruction.
Having heard that sound, one understands its meaning.
What is the meaning of sound?
That which is entirely unclassifiable and inexpressible is the meaning of sound.
The meaning of tranquility is the meaning of all sounds.
That bodhisattva practices this meaning accordingly; hearing all sounds, they do not give rise to dependence, because all phenomena are fundamentally non-arising.

"If there are Buddhas, World-Honored Ones, currently living and residing in countless worlds throughout the ten directions, whatever Dharma those Buddhas preach, that bodhisattva hears it all with the divine ear, without obstruction or hindrance."
Without grasping at the sense-sphere of sound, they hear all sounds of the Dharma being taught; having heard them, they receive and uphold them without any loss.
How is it that there is no forgetting?
If a bodhisattva were to grasp even a single phrase, then forgetting might occur.
Because that bodhisattva does not grasp even a single phrase, he has no forgetfulness.

Whether that bodhisattva hears of outflowing phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) or outflow-free phenomena (*anāsrava-dharma*); whether he hears of permanent phenomena or impermanent phenomena; whether he hears of mundane phenomena or supramundane phenomena; whether he hears of wholesome or unwholesome phenomena, increasing or decreasing phenomena; or whether he hears of the teachings of the śrāvakas, the pratyekabuddhas, or the Mahāyāna—all these phenomena are of one essence and one flavor.
Thus practicing in accordance with the Dharma means that, having heard the teaching, one attains the flavor of detachment; hearing all dharmas and all objects, one neither grasps nor clings to them.
Furthermore, hearing the Dharma, one does not dwell in or cling to any signs, but practices in conformity with all dharmas and does not practice in conformity with what is non-dharmic.
What is the Dharma? What is non-Dharma?
The Dharma is named detachment from desire;

the Dharma is named signlessness; the Dharma is named unconditioned; the Dharma is named placelessness. It is beyond analogy, free from defilement, and without attainment; it is neither born nor produced—this is called the Dharma.

If one recollects, discriminates, conceives, observes, or engages in conceptual proliferation regarding such dharmas by grasping at them as things to be accepted or rejected, this is called "non-dharma.
O Vaśavartin King!

That bodhisattva takes only the meaning and does not take the words; he does not listen to or hear the Dharma for the sake of grasping the words, but listens to the Dharma for the sake of grasping the meaning.
What is meant by "grasping the meaning"?

If one perceives the meaning of emptiness without grasping or attachment, the meaning of signlessness without grasping or attachment, and the meaning of wishlessness without grasping or attachment—this is called grasping the meaning.

If he listens to the Dharma by grasping its meaning, yet does not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding that grasped meaning, and does not even discriminate against non-discrimination—in this way, a bodhisattva listens to the Dharma in the presence of the Buddhas.
"Furthermore, O Vegeśvara!
That bodhisattva conforms to the meaning of the sūtras of definitive meaning (nītārtha), and does not conform to the meaning of the sūtras of non-definitive meaning (neyārtha).
What is the meaning of that 'definitive meaning'?"

Because the meaning of all those sūtras consists entirely of the definitive meaning of the sūtras, because they are all taught in accordance with a non-contradictory sense, and because the meaning of all definitive sūtras is inexpressible; thus, one practices in accordance with the meaning of the definitive sūtras.
If one does not act in accordance with the meaning of the definitive sūtras, then it is not the definitive meaning.
For what reason is it not of definitive meaning?
If the meaning of a sūtra that is not of definitive meaning does not accord with the meaning of a sūtra that is of definitive meaning, it is inconsistent with that which is of definitive meaning.
For what reason are they not in accord?
Because they do not conform and thus depart from the practice of those dharmas.
That which is said to "conform" refers to conformity with sound; however, the sūtras of definitive meaning (nītārtha) do not conform to sound.
Why is this? Because that definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) is inexpressible, it is without any point of attachment.
In this way, the bodhisattva skillfully knows that all non-definitive teachings (*neyārtha*) are just like the definitive meaning.
“Vīryaketu, this meaning accords with the meaning of the sūtras of definitive meaning; it likewise accords with the meaning of all sūtras of definitive meaning.”
"Furthermore, O Veṣṭhita-rāja!
After that bodhisattva has heard the Dharma from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, he takes up only wisdom (jñāna) and does not take up consciousness (vijñāna). Why is this?

Because it is known by consciousness, because it is like an illusion, because it cannot be grasped, because it lacks intrinsic nature, because it is formless, because it is invisible, and because it is unobstructed—if one knows it in this way, that is knowledge through wisdom.
Therefore, the bodhisattva takes up only wisdom (*jñāna*) and does not take up consciousness (*vijñāna*), for consciousness is known by another.
Knowing consciousness in this way, he is attached to neither consciousness nor wisdom; he explains the suchness of wisdom through the suchness of consciousness.

"Vīryendrarāja! If a bodhisattva grasps only wisdom and does not grasp consciousness, he does not preach the dharma of consciousness to sentient beings; having attained this supernormal power of the divine ear, he realizes this realm of wisdom."
"Furthermore, O Veṣthila!
When that bodhisattva-pudgala speaks in accordance with the Dharma, he grasps only the Dharma and does not grasp the person. Why is this? "
Vīryendrarāja!
If there were truly such a person, sentient beings would ultimately be incapable of purification and incapable of liberation within the Buddha-dharma.
Vīryendrarāja!
If this is so, then all phenomena are ultimately devoid of a person.
It is in reliance upon worldly convention that the Buddha speaks of a "person," yet in reality, all phenomena are entirely without a person.
In this way, the bodhisattva grasps only the Dharma and does not grasp at persons. O Virajendra,
"Dharma" is a name for the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), and this Dharma-realm is called the realm of non-arising (anutpādadhatu).
Vīryaketu, that which is the non-arising realm is called the non-emerging realm. Vīryaketu!
That which is called "name" (nāma) is so named because it cannot be expressed; why is this?
Because one knows various phenomena (dharma) by means of their respective names, yet within those various phenomena, no name can be found.
If [the ultimate] cannot be apprehended, one speaks words out of accord with human sentiment; all such speech is spoken in accordance with worldly convention.
If I understand the words, they are the Buddha’s words;
if conceptual characteristics arise, they are not the Buddha’s words.
The Buddha’s speech is without intention; because it is without speech, it is called the Buddha’s speech.
If one enters the Buddha’s speech, one enters non-speech;
if one enters non-speech, one enters the Buddha’s speech.
If one wishes to enter into speech, one should enter into the Buddha’s speech;
yet if one wishes to enter into the Buddha’s speech by grasping at the speech of the person who speaks it or grasping at the speech that expresses the Dharma,
if one grasps in such a manner, one does not enter into the Buddha’s speech.
Where is there neither duality nor non-duality?
That is the word of the Buddha.
Where is there sound and where is there the absence of sound?
"That is not the word of the Buddha.
That which is neither expressible nor inexpressible—that is the word of the Buddha.
Thus it is, O Vigraharāja!"

If a bodhisattva enters into the Buddha’s word, they are said to have attained the supernormal power of the divine ear; by accords with all sounds, they realize the Dharma and attain the Buddha-bodhi.
“Vīryendrarāja! This is the second supernormal knowledge of a bodhisattva, namely, the divine ear (divyaśrotra).
Furthermore, Vīryendrarāja!”

Furthermore, the bodhisattva attains the supernormal knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*), whereby he knows the minds and intentions of other sentient beings and other individuals (*pudgala*).
Thus entering into a great assembly to preach the Dharma, he first observes the minds of the gathering in this way:
"Which sentient beings possess what kind of profound intention?"
"What is their practice?
What are its causes and characteristics?
Having thus observed, he teaches the Dharma as appropriate; because his own mind is pure, he is able to enter all assemblies with a pure mind.
"Vīryendrarāja! For example, because a mirror-disk is pure, it manifests such colors as blue, yellow, and so forth;
whether it be shapes or characteristics, they are seen exactly as they are, neither increasing nor decreasing, because the mirror-disk is pure."
Yet that mirror-disk makes no discriminations while manifesting all images. "Vikrāntarāja!

In this same way, the Bodhisattva’s own mind is like the pure wheel of the white dharma-realm; although he knows all the mental activities and various diverse births of sentient beings, the mind of that Bodhisattva remains unimpaired."
If anyone among that assembly wishes to practice, he knows that person’s mind and knows the mind free from desire.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the mind is without the defilement of desire.
Within that assembly, there may be those whose conduct is characterized by anger or delusion; yet he knows their minds and knows the mind free from delusion.
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the mind is devoid of anger and delusion.
“Furthermore, if there is a person who believes in the Śrāvaka-yāna, the Bodhisattva can know that person’s mental activities without the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) diminishing;
if there is another person who believes in the Pratyekabuddha-yāna, the Bodhisattva can know that person’s mental activities without the dharma-realm decreasing;
and if there is yet another person within that assembly whose mental activities belong to the Mahāyāna, the Bodhisattva can know that person’s mental activities without the dharma-realm increasing.”

Having known the realms of the mental activities of those sentient beings, he preaches the Dharma for them; yet, without discriminating the fundamental nature of the mind, he teaches the Dharma as appropriate to cause them to abide in the various vehicles. Within the non-disruption of all realms, he thoroughly knows the manifold types of conduct of all sentient beings.
That bodhisattva observes his own mind with his own mind:
"It is neither a continuity of mind, nor is it subject to annihilation.
Yet, by means of that continuous mind, the bodhisattva is able to universally know the minds of all sentient beings in the same way; if it is the realm of mind, he knows that realm as it truly is.
The dharma-realm is likewise neither one nor two.
"In this way, O Vigraharāja,

when a bodhisattva attains the wisdom of the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others, by virtue of having attained such powers, he is called a 'possessor of powers' (abhijñā-vant) and is recognized by all devas and humans."
"Furthermore, O Viravikrama!

A bodhisattva further attains the supernormal knowledge of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛtijñāna*). By means of the faculty of samādhi, he is able to know the past lives of himself and others throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, remembering them without forgetfulness; having known this, he then expounds the Dharma."
He recollects in this way:

"In such-and-such a place, I had such-and-such a name; I was born in such-and-such a manner, had such-and-such a lifespan, experienced such-and-such pleasure, and experienced such-and-such suffering."

"With one's own mind, one is able to know the minds of other sentient beings; one knows the prior roots of goodness of these sentient beings, one knows the power of the causes of these sentient beings' roots of goodness, one knows the power of the conditions for these sentient beings' roots of goodness, one knows the cause of the Śrāvaka vehicle of these sentient beings, one knows the cause of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle of these sentient beings, and one knows that these sentient beings possess the cause of the Mahāyāna. Having known the prior causes and conditions of those sentient beings, one then preaches the Dharma to such sentient beings according to what is appropriate."
That bodhisattva knows his own past lives; having known his past lives, he is further able to know the full extent of his original cultivation.

He knows for himself how many buddhas he served in the past to plant various roots of goodness, and whether those roots of goodness were previously dedicated toward the aspiration for *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
Having thus recollected those roots of goodness, he further makes a vow.

That bodhisattva, mindful of his past lives, does not conceptually differentiate among any dharmas of the past; he is neither attached to nor grasps them. He does not conceptually differentiate between subsequent and preceding actions, nor between preceding and subsequent actions; regarding all dharmas as a state of non-differentiation, whether going or coming, he remains thus.
“Having recollected past lives, the bodhisattva nevertheless neither grasps nor clings to the past;
although he knows the future, he likewise neither grasps nor clings to the future.”
Knowing that all phenomena have no before, no after, and no middle, they do not discriminate, do not grasp, and do not cling.
That Bodhisattva thus recollects the past lives of sentient beings; he is able to know how their prior and subsequent forms are detached;
likewise, he is able to know how their prior and subsequent feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all detached.
"Furthermore, the Bodhisattva is able to know that all phenomena—whether the five aggregates, or those preceding, following, or intermediate—are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature.
O King Vikrāntarāja!

Once that Bodhisattva has recollected his past lives, all the roots of goodness cultivated in the past will fully increase, and all karmic actions performed in the past will be completely extinguished."
Why is this? Because karma does not perish; therefore, one is able to know.

When a bodhisattva has thus accomplished that knowledge, they have faith and understanding that all conditioned phenomena are like dreams—for example, as in a dream one sees birth, sees death, sees suffering, and sees pleasure.
The Bodhisattva’s faith and understanding regarding all conditioned phenomena is likewise so.

Having attained such faith and understanding, they do not undergo suffering within that cycle of birth and death; furthermore, they give rise to a heart of compassion for sentient beings and realize that all dharmas do not give rise to the characteristic of arising.
"Furthermore, that bodhisattva has such a thought:
'I have known that throughout many thousands of kalpas of birth and death in the world of the past, all things are without reality, and thus I have neither craved nor clung to them;
likewise, I know that the birth and death of all sentient beings in the world is illusory and unreal, and thus I neither crave nor cling to it.'"
"If it were not real, then in that state of unreality, the great would not arise, and the great would not be real. "O Virasena!
Having recollected his past lives, that bodhisattva truly sees that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are entirely impermanent."
Why is this? That bodhisattva recollects that the pleasures of past universal monarchs (cakravartin) are phenomena subject to impermanence and decay;
he recollects that the pleasures of past Śakra kings are likewise phenomena subject to impermanence and decay.
He recollects the past bliss of the Brahma Kings, realizing that it is a phenomenon subject to impermanence and decay.
He contemplates and recollects the adornments of the worlds of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; the adornment of the merits of the śrāvakas; and the adornment of the merits of the bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, he recollects those Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, as being fully endowed with the rūpakāya, and the Tathāgatas as being fully endowed with the turning of the wheel of Dharma.
Having recollected this, he does not become attached; he completely relinquishes all conditioned phenomena and everything that is grasped. Why is this?
Because that bodhisattva possesses such a mind:
"If those Buddha-worlds are thus superior and the Buddha’s form-body is thus superior, they too are impermanent and subject to the law of exhaustion and cessation;
that which is encompassed by me is likewise entirely impermanent."
He further reflects:
"All conditioned phenomena are thus; all are impermanent, yet sentient beings conceive the notion of permanence.
Thus, the Bodhisattva gives rise to great compassion for sentient beings and completely relinquishes attachment to all dharmas.
"In this way, O Viravikrama!
This is the fourth supernormal knowledge of a bodhisattva.

When that bodhisattva has accomplished this knowledge, he knows that all phenomena are impermanent; with right mental attention, he takes up existence and brings sentient beings to maturity. Although he takes up existence, he does not become attached to it; the bodhisattva, being detached from existence, yet assumes various forms of existence to mature sentient beings."
"Furthermore, Viravikrama!
What is the Bodhisattva’s heroic display of supernormal powers? Viravikrama!"
Because that bodhisattva possesses mastery over the mind, they attain the noble bases of supernormal power—namely, aspiration, diligence, tranquility, and resolute conviction.

Although the supernormal powers attained by that bodhisattva are conditioned phenomena, that person aspires to be able to reach all Buddha-worlds, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, in a single moment of thought.
Having arrived at that place, the sentient beings there see the body of the Bodhisattva, yet the Bodhisattva’s body does not move from this place;
the sentient beings there see and hear him preaching the Dharma, yet his preaching of the Dharma here is uninterrupted.
“Vīryendrarāja! This is the sovereign power of a bodhisattva’s supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā-vikrīḍita*); by means of these supernormal knowledges, he disciplines sentient beings.

If there are sentient beings—whether gods or humans—who conceive the notion of permanence, he manifests the conflagration at the end of an eon (*kalpa*). They see the trichiliocosm entirely ablaze, yet that world is not actually destroyed by fire.

If there are arrogant sentient beings, he displays a vajra in his hand to the yakṣas and manifests vajra-flames to inspire great terror in them; those who were conceited immediately shatter their pride and prostrate themselves before him.
If there are sentient beings who have faith in a Wheel-Turning King, he manifests in the form and attire of a Wheel-Turning King and preaches the Dharma for them;
if there are sentient beings who have faith in Śakra, the King of Devas, he manifests in the appearance of Śakra and preaches the Dharma for them;
if there are sentient beings who have faith in Brahmā, he manifests in the form and appearance of Brahmā and preaches the Dharma for them.
If there are sentient beings who have faith in the Māra-king, he immediately manifests in the form and color of the Māra-king to preach the Dharma for them;
if there are sentient beings who have faith in the Tathāgata, he immediately manifests in the form and color of the Tathāgata to preach the Dharma for them.

If there are sentient beings who should see the Bodhisattva dwelling in mid-air, sitting cross-legged and emitting light from his body, the Bodhisattva will then remain in the air, radiating light from his body as he preaches the Dharma for them.

"If there are sentient beings who give rise to faith and understanding regarding great and supreme matters, he immediately displays the adornments of banners and canopies, the adornments of flower garlands and banners, the adornments of victory banners and pennants, complete with sets of bell-garlands and the delights of incense and hundreds of thousands of kinds of music. Having displayed these things, he then preaches the Dharma."

If there are sentient beings who should see the trichiliocosm merged into a single ocean, with *utpala*, *kumuda*, and *puṇḍarīka* flowers covering the surface of the water, and upon those lotuses are lion thrones, whereupon one sits and preaches the Dharma—then he manifests such a scene and preaches the Dharma for them.
If there are sentient beings who should see the Bodhisattva dwelling upon the summit of Mount Sumeru and teaching with a Brahma-voice, he manifests himself to them and preaches the Dharma;
if there are sentient beings who should not see his body but hear only the Bodhisattva’s great voice preaching, he manifests himself to them and preaches the Dharma;
if there are sentient beings who should see the body of a nāga or the body of a gandharva, the Bodhisattva then manifests a voice corresponding to song and preaches the Dharma to them.
If there are sentient beings who should see dragon wheels, hear the sounds of thunder and lightning, or witness falling rain, he manifests these for them and preaches the Dharma.

If there are sentient beings who are hungry, thirsty, or exhausted, he provides them with celestial food and drink in abundance, causing their bodies to be fully satiated and all their needs to be joyfully met, and only then preaches the Dharma to them.

If there are sentient beings within the hells who constantly undergo great suffering, he uses his supernormal powers to extinguish the fires of hell and infuses strength into every pore of their skin; once they have attained happiness, he then preaches the Dharma to them.

"If there are sentient beings who are blind or deprived of their eyes, he uses his supernormal powers to grant them the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), and only after they have regained the faculty of sight does he preach the Dharma to them.

If there are sentient beings who are deaf or deprived of their faculty of hearing, he uses his supernormal powers to enable them to regain the faculty of hearing, and only then does he preach the Dharma to them.
If there are sentient beings afflicted by various illnesses, he uses his supernormal powers to eliminate those many ailments; once they are freed from illness, he then preaches the Dharma to them."

"If there are sentient beings who are about to be killed and their lives are on the verge of being severed, he uses his supernormal powers to employ various skillful means to steal away that person so they do not incur the sin; or, having ransomed their lives by giving them wealth, he then preaches the Dharma for them."

"If there are sentient beings whose physical forms are inferior, whose faculties are incomplete, or who—due to low birth—are fearful, ashamed, or mentally and physically debased, [the Buddha] uses his supernormal powers to cause all their limbs and members to become complete, temporarily manifesting a body superior to their own, and only then does he preach the Dharma for them."

"If there are sentient beings who are deaf and mute within their wombs, born inherently dull-witted, or lying in excrement and urine, he first provides them with medical treatment; having manifested a palace adorned with jewels through his supernatural powers and seated them therein, he then preaches the Dharma to them; and once their minds and wisdom have been awakened, he then preaches the Dharma."

"If there are beings, whether yet unborn or already born, whose faculties are not yet matured, he uses his supernormal powers to bring those faculties to maturity before preaching the Dharma to them. O Vaśavartin!"
At that time, having accomplished such supernormal powers, the Bodhisattva further possesses inconceivable supernormal powers for preaching the Dharma.

If there are sentient beings who, with faith and understanding, enter the discipline of the Dharma under the sun and moon, he uses his supernormal power to place all the suns and moons within the three thousand great thousandfold world systems upon the palm of his hand and hurls them beyond immeasurable and boundless worlds. All sentient beings who are to be delivered see the suns and moons traveling through the air, yet those suns and moons remain unmoved from their original positions.

Furthermore, he is able to place Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges upon the tip of a single hair and hurl them to the Brahma world; thereafter, he hurls them beyond immeasurable and boundless worlds, yet all sentient beings do not perceive or know whether they have come or gone, nor do they have any thought of coming or going.
Furthermore, with a single breath, that bodhisattva can extinguish the fires of the kalpa-conflagration throughout immeasurable worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Moreover, by sitting cross-legged just once, that bodhisattva can instantly cause his body to reach Buddha-worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva is able to cover the sun and the moon with both hands, illuminating the world entirely with his own radiance as he preaches the Dharma.
"O King Vikrāntarāja!

That bodhisattva sat cross-legged before the Tathāgata and, conceiving a mind of longing to make offerings to the Tathāgata, was immediately able to scatter various exquisite flowers, equal in size to Mount Sumeru, over the body of the Tathāgata, causing all the flowers to cover and obscure the Tathāgata so that only his half-body remained visible.
If one were to transform all the forests of the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system into lamps for illumination as previously offered, one could do so at will.

When it rains, one can cause fire to be seen and manifest one’s own body such that all sentient beings see it everywhere; according to the various inclinations and understandings of those sentient beings, they see whatever form it may be—whether one manifests one’s own body as the body of Śakra, or as the body of Brahmā, or as the body of a śrāvaka, or as the body of a pratyekabuddha.

“Vīryaketu, this is the Bodhisattva’s prowess of supernormal powers (*abhijñā-vikrīḍita*): namely, seeing with the divine eye without obstruction, hearing with the pure divine ear without obstruction, knowing the mental activities of all sentient beings through wisdom, and being able to recollect incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpa*). To be able to manifest all supernormal powers is called the prowess of supernormal powers.”
“Vīryendrarāja! As for what is called ‘supernormal power’ (abhijñā), why is it named such?

It is the supernormal power of universally seeing the activities of all Buddhas; the supernormal power of knowing the faculties of all sentient beings; the supernormal power of surpassing the laws and discipline of the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Dharma and Vinaya of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the discipline of the Mahāyāna; the supernormal power of emerging from sitting in meditation; the supernormal power of the wisdom that matures all sentient beings; the supernormal power of departing with correct knowledge; the supernormal power of skillful means; the supernormal power of the vows of giving; and the supernormal power of the vows of morality, patience, diligence, meditation, and wisdom. Because it destroys Māra, gathers in Māra, and brings the roots of goodness to fulfillment, it is therefore called ‘supernormal power.’”
"Furthermore, O King Viraja!

When a bodhisattva attains supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), he becomes known by others for his physical form—such as its blue color and other qualities—as well as for his majesty, fame, power, clan, lineage, wealth, and retinue; therefore, it is called 'supernormal power.'
"Furthermore, O King Viraja!

When a bodhisattva attains supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), he knows all things: devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans and non-humans, Śakra the king of gods, universal monarchs (*cakravartin*), the lords of the Brahma-world, arhats, and the Perfectly Awakened Ones (*samyaksaṃbuddha*). For this reason, it is called 'supernormal power.'"

“Vīryendrarāja! This is the supernormal power (abhijñā) of a bodhisattva; by means of this power, the bodhisattva does not retreat from their original vow and is able to demonstrate all dharmas to others. Vīryendrarāja!”
What is the "swift mastery of wisdom"?
O King Swift Mastery!

The swift mastery of wisdom refers to the knowledge of the aggregates (skandha), the knowledge of the elements (dhātu), the knowledge of the sense bases (āyatana), the knowledge of causes and conditions (pratītyasamutpāda), and the knowledge of the true realities (satya).
“Vīryendrarāja! What is the knowledge of the aggregates?
It is the knowledge that form is empty—that the prior limit of form is empty, the posterior limit of form is empty, and the middle limit of form is empty.

Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are all likewise: the prior limit of consciousness is empty, the posterior limit of consciousness is empty, and the middle limit of consciousness is empty.
This emptiness of the five aggregates is called ultimate emptiness; knowing this emptiness of the aggregates is therefore termed "knowledge of the aggregates."
“Vīryendrarāja! What is the knowledge of the elements?
It is the dharma-element of the earth element, the dharma-element of the water element, the dharma-element of the fire element, and the dharma-element of the wind element.”
Why is this? Because these four elements and the dharma-element are one element—namely, the space-element.
Furthermore, the dharma-element is itself an element; it is neither the earth-element, nor the water-element, nor the fire-element, nor the wind-element.

Why is this? Because the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu) is not a different realm, the realm of phenomena is non-dual, the realm of phenomena is unborn, the realm of phenomena is unstained, and the realm of phenomena is perfectly pure; it is as the realm of phenomena, as the realm of self, as the realm of sentient beings, as the realm of life, as the realm of persons (pudgala), as the realm of birth and death, and as the realm of nirvana.

That realm is the desire realm, that realm is the form realm, that realm is the formless realm, that realm is the conditioned realm, and that realm is the unconditioned realm; therefore, it is called the realm of nirvana.
If it is the wisdom of the dharma-realm, then likewise, the wisdom of the form-realm is not different from the wisdom of causes and conditions;
therefore, it is called "wisdom of the realms.
"Vīryaketu-rāja! What is the wisdom of entry?"
Vīryaketu! The intrinsic nature of the eye is unborn, unarisen, and without a creator. Vīryaketu!
In this way, the natures of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are unarisen, unproduced, and without an agent.

O Virasena! Because that eye has no master, there is no seer; because that ear has no master, there is no hearer; because that nose has no master, there is no smeller; because that tongue has no master, there is no taster; because that body has no master, there is no feeler; and because that mind has no master, there is no knower.
Vīryaketu-rāja! The eye does not see forms;
the ear does not hear sounds; the nose does not smell odors; the tongue does not taste flavors; the body does not feel tangibles; and the mind does not cognize phenomena.
Why is this? The eye is devoid of sentience, like grass, like wood, like a wall, like a clod of earth;
likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—all are devoid of sentience, like grass, like wood, like a wall, like a clod of earth.
“Vīryendrarāja! The eye is neither defiled nor undefiled;
likewise, the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind—all are neither defiled nor undefiled.”
Why is this? Because the intrinsic nature of the eye is by its very nature free from defilement;
likewise, the intrinsic natures of the ear, nose, tongue, body, and mind are also thus, being by their very nature free from defilement.
“Vīryendrarāja! If one knows all the *āyatanas* in this way, the mind attains detachment from desire; therefore, it is called the wisdom of the *āyatanas*.

If one knows in this way that the aggregates (*skandhas*), elements (*dhātus*), and *āyatanas* are neither produced nor cease, and having thus entered ultimate *nirvāṇa*, one then takes up the arising and passing away of the aggregates, elements, and *āyatanas*, yet does not abandon them as they are—just like the aggregates, elements, and *āyatanas* themselves.”

This "leap of wisdom" knows the characteristics and the essence of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; it relinquishes them all, yet continues to traverse the three realms without being stained or attached. It manifests birth and death, yet remains free from birth and death—this is the leap of wisdom.
“Vīryendrarāja! What is the knowledge of causal conditions?
Conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations; yet ignorance does not think:”
"I can produce volitional formations.
Conditioned by volitional formations, consciousness arises; yet volitional formations do not think:
"I can produce consciousness."
"Consciousness conditions name-and-form, yet consciousness does not think:
'I produce name-and-form.
Name-and-form conditions the six sense bases, yet name-and-form does not think:"
"I give rise to the six sense bases.
Conditioned by the six sense bases is contact; yet the six sense bases do not think, "I am able to produce contact."
"Contact conditions feeling, yet contact does not think:
'I am able to produce feeling.
Feeling conditions craving, yet feeling also does not think:"
"I am able to produce craving.
Craving conditions grasping, yet craving does not think:
"I am able to produce grasping."
"Grasping conditions existence, yet grasping does not think:
'I can produce existence.
Existence conditions birth, yet existence also does not think:"
"I am able to produce birth.
Birth conditions old age and death, yet birth does not think:
"I produce old age and death."
"Vīryaketu, when a bodhisattva observes dependent origination in this way, they are free from all views; they possess neither the view of nihilism nor the view of eternalism."

"He thus knows that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions; yet, when he investigates those causes and conditions in this manner, they cannot be apprehended. Thus, regarding causes and conditions, he attains the wisdom of causes and conditions."
How does one attain wisdom?
Through the equality of these two—causes and conditions and non-arising. Such equality is empty, signless, and wishless; thus, all twelve links of dependent origination are entirely equal.
If one awakens to such equality, all phenomena are equal in their causes and conditions; such causes and conditions are, in fact, not causes and conditions.

Because not even the slightest phenomenon arises within those causes and conditions, they are called "causes and conditions. To know that non-arising is also a cause and condition is termed "knowledge of causes and conditions."
“Knowledge and ignorance—these phenomena are non-dual; one who knows this is said to possess the wisdom of dependent origination.
Volitional formations and non-formations—these phenomena are non-dual; one who knows this is said to possess the wisdom of dependent origination.
Consciousness and non-consciousness—these phenomena are non-dual; one who knows this is said to possess the wisdom of dependent origination.”
Name-and-form and non-name-and-form—these phenomena are not two; one who knows this is said to possess the wisdom of dependent origination.
The six sense bases and non-six-sense-bases—these phenomena are not two; one who knows this is said to possess the wisdom of dependent origination.

Just as the six sense bases and non-six-sense-bases are not two, so too are contact and non-contact not two; feeling and non-feeling are not two; craving and non-craving are not two; grasping and non-grasping are not two; existence and non-existence are not two; birth and non-birth are not two; and aging-and-death and non-aging-and-death are not two. One who knows this is said to possess the wisdom of dependent origination.

"Just as the conditions are, so too those conditions are empty and selfless; just as those conditions neither come nor go, so too those conditions are false and unreal; just as those conditions are without grasping or that which is grasped, so too these conditions are without activity and without marks. To know them thus is called the knowledge of conditions."

“If one sees dependent origination, one does not see ignorance, nor does one see volitional formations, nor consciousness, nor name-and-form, nor the six sense bases, nor contact, nor feeling, nor craving, nor clinging, nor existence, nor birth, nor aging and death. To see in this way is to see dependent origination;
to see dependent origination is to see the Dharma.”
What kind of phenomena does one see?
One sees the phenomena of detachment from desire.
From what kind of desire is one detached?

Among all phenomena, there are various kinds of views and desires; because one is free from such desires, it is called "freedom from desire. Those phenomena thus perceived neither increase nor decrease;

such perception is *tathatā* (suchness), which cannot be attained and is unstained. Such perception is the *dharmadhātu* (dharma-realm), which is neither destroyed nor established. Such perception is the *bhūtakoṭi* (limit of reality), which is not pierced. Although such perception sees, it is a non-seeing.
Such a vision is not seen by the fleshly eye, nor by the divine eye, nor by the wisdom eye.
Why is this? Because the fleshly eye does not perceive; since it does not perceive, it does not see.
The divine eye is conditioned; because it is conditioned, it does not see the unconditioned, and for this reason it does not see.
The wisdom eye does not see, because it does not engage in conceptual discrimination; because it does not engage in conceptual discrimination, it likewise cannot see.

“Vīryaketu, when a bodhisattva perceives all phenomena in this way, they perceive the Tathāgata. It is not by perceiving form; it is not by perceiving feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness; it is not by perceiving marks; it is not by perceiving the dharma-realm; it is not by perceiving morality, concentration, wisdom, liberation, nor even the knowledge and vision of liberation; it is not by perceiving the past, the future, or the present. To perceive in such a manner is to perceive the Tathāgata.”
