Translated by the Brahmin Gautama Prajñāruci of the Northern Wei Dynasty.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Veṣṭhila addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One! If there were such a thing as a dharma, could one see the dharma?
If there were such a thing as seeing the dharma, could one see the Tathāgata?”
The Buddha said, “There is.
For what reason?”
Vīryendrarāja! The characteristic of form (*rūpa*) is non-arising; its intrinsic nature is non-arising. To see form in this way is to see the Tathāgata.

Likewise, the characteristics of feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are all non-arising; their intrinsic nature is non-arising. To see consciousness in this way is to see the Tathāgata.
The precepts possess conditioned characteristics yet are unconditioned; seeing the precepts in this way is to see the Tathāgata.
When samādhi is equanimous, there is pure vision; it was in this manner that I attained pure vision under Dīpaṃkara Buddha.

“I attained the conditions for seeing that Buddha through the causes and conditions of seeing; by means of seeing those causes and conditions, I immediately saw the Dharma; and because I saw the Dharma, I saw the Tathāgata.
The Bodhisattva Veṣṭhitarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"When Dīpaṃkara Buddha came, and all the Tathāgatas who followed him— how were they seen?
The Buddha said,
"Vikrāntagāmin!"
All are seen through the discrimination of form and characteristics; they do not see the Dharma-body.
O King Vikrāntarāja!
I shall speak for you; you should now know this:
Since I first resolved to attain bodhicitta, I have not seen another Buddha except for Dīpaṃkara. Why is this?
It is because I do not see the Tathāgata through the perception of physical form; rather, I see the Tathāgata through pure vision.
“Vīryendrarāja! A bodhisattva who wishes to see the Buddha in this way should do so as I saw the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, by means of a single dharma.
What is that one dharma?
As is my body, so too is the body of that Dīpaṃkara;
as is the body of Dīpaṃkara, so too is my body.
One body, one dharma—realizing the non-duality of dharmas and not discriminating this realization is the wisdom of dependent origination.
If one perceives causes and conditions, one perceives the Dharma;
by perceiving the Dharma, one perceives the Tathāgata.

If, in all places where the mind arises, one realizes their cessation—neither entering nirvāṇa nor attaining birth and death—this is called "mastery" (vikrīḍita), as taught through the wisdom of skillful means.
"What is this knowledge of the true reality?
What is it for the śrāvaka?
At the time of truth, one touches liberation."
In this way, at the time of reality, the bodhisattva also attains liberation without contact; this is "mastery" (vikrīḍita).
As for the pratyekabuddha, what is it?
At the time of reality, he attains liberation through contact.
In this way, at the time of reality, the bodhisattva also attains liberation without contact; this is prowess (*vikrīḍita*).
"The knower of the truth of reality" refers to one who knows that suffering is neither a truth nor a reality.
What is wisdom? It is the knowledge of unreality, because it arises from the cessation of infinite inversions.
To know that suffering does not arise—that it is ultimately non-arising—and to know suffering in this way as non-arising, is called the knowledge of suffering.
"What is the abandonment of origination?
One abandins origination in accordance with the nature of that origination.
What is called 'origination'?"
It is called "accumulation" because it accumulates; one abandons accumulation with equanimity.
If future accumulation is abandoned in the future, this is the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); there is not even the slightest phenomenon that is produced or abandoned.
“The fetter of craving gives rise to existence; by severing that fetter of craving, it is called the ‘severance of craving.
What is the cessation of suffering?
If that nature of the arising of suffering is ultimately extinguished, such that no phenomenon remains to perish, this is called cessation.”
If all signs of objective reference were extinguished, this would be inconsistent with the meaning; what dharma could arise?
What dharma could cease?
What, then, would constitute the Path?

That which is called the Way—whether wholesome or unwholesome, with outflows or without outflows, defiled or undefiled, conditioned or unconditioned—is entirely unapprehendable; this is what is called the Way.
Equanimity is called the path, because all phenomena are truly real;
tranquility is called the path, because all fevers have been entirely abandoned;
security is called the path, because one does not depart from all skillful means.
The untainted is called the Path because all outflows have been exhausted;
non-activity is called the Path because those with discriminatory views cannot practice it;
ease of practice is called the Path because it is what can be practiced by those who engage in correct cultivation.
"Non-abandonment is called the Way, for it was not abandoned by the Tathāgatas of the past;
freedom from marks is called the Way, for it can sever all doubts.
If one does not enter into either of these two regarding this Way, this is what is called attaining the Way."
If one understands the meaning of these Four Truths in this way, it is called the knowledge of the ultimate truth (*bhūtārtha-jñāna*).

If, regarding these Four Truths, one does not give rise to longing for the vows of the Śrāvaka vehicle or the Pratyekabuddha vehicle—that is what is termed the "leap of ultimate knowledge" (*bhūtārtha-jñāna-vaśitā*).
"Furthermore, O Vigourous King!
One who possesses the vigor of wisdom knows the vehicle of the śrāvakas, yet does not grasp it and does not abide in it;
one knows the vehicle of the pratyekabuddhas, yet does not grasp it and does not abide in it—this is the vigor of wisdom."
"Furthermore, O Vigour King!

As for the 'Vigour of Wisdom,' if one, with a single mind, universally knows the minds of all sentient beings, and with a single mind, realizes and universally knows the essence of the minds of all sentient beings—whether as mind or as wisdom—and these two minds do not arise alternately, this is the Vigour of Wisdom."
"Furthermore, O King Vikrāmin!
One who possesses the vigor of wisdom perceives the past without obstruction or hindrance, yet the mind does not turn toward the past;
he perceives the future without obstruction or hindrance, yet the mind does not turn toward the future or the past."

To possess knowledge and vision that are unobstructed and unhindered regarding the present, while remaining free from conceptual proliferation concerning the past, future, and present minds—this is the agility of wisdom.
"Furthermore, O Vegeśvara! As for the 'leap of wisdom' (jñāna-vega):

if one knows through the knowledge of exhaustion (kṣayajñāna), yet also knows that the practice of roots of goodness is not exhausted; and if one knows through the knowledge of non-arising (anutpādajñāna) while also knowing the origin [of suffering], this is the leap of wisdom."
"Furthermore, O Vejayanta-rāja!

As for the 'swift display of wisdom' (jñāna-vega-prasarana): if all phenomena are ultimately quiescent, and one knows that all phenomena do not arise from other causes and conditions, yet by the power of wisdom does not enter nirvāṇa—for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to maturity—this is the bodhisattva’s swift display of wisdom."
"In this way, Viravikrama,
a bodhisattva who wishes to display the prowess of this wisdom should skillfully perform the deeds of wisdom and must not perform deeds of pride."

What is the karma of pride? All intentional mental activities are the karma of pride; all cognitive activities are the karma of pride; all volitional mental activities are the karma of pride. All practices of seeking pleasure, all acts of giving based on views, and all observances of precepts based on conceptualization are the karma of pride. All forms of patience practiced based on the distinction between self and others are the karma of pride; all forms of diligence that arise from the mind’s conceptual discrimination are the karma of pride.
Even the wisdom that discriminates the body is likewise the karma of pride. All such things are the karma of pride.
"All instances of conceiving the pride of 'I' are karmas of arrogance:
to think, 'I am a bodhisattva,' is itself a karma of arrogance."
"I am a bodhisattva who abides"—
this is an act of pride;
"I am able to ensure that the lineage of the Buddha, the lineage of the Dharma, and the lineage of the Saṅgha are not severed."
To say, "This is the karma of pride";
to say, "I perform acts for the benefit of sentient beings," this is the karma of pride.

“Those sentient beings who have not yet crossed over, I shall cause them to cross over; those who are not yet liberated, I shall cause them to be liberated; those who are not yet comforted, I shall be able to comfort them; and those who have not yet attained nirvāṇa, I shall cause them to attain nirvāṇa.”
"This is the karma of pride:
'I practice giving; I maintain the precepts; I am patient; I practice diligence; I practice meditation; I possess wisdom.'"
"This is an act of pride;
'I practice loving-kindness, I practice compassion, I practice sympathetic joy, I practice equanimity'—
this is an act of pride."
"I practice few desires, I practice contentment, I practice seclusion, and I practice non-attachment"—this is the karma of conceit.
"I practice the dhūta austerities, I practice correctly in empty and quiet places, and I engage in recollection and discrimination. This is the karma of conceit.
"This is the karma of pride;
'I practice the practice of emptiness, I practice the practice of signlessness, I practice the practice of wishlessness'—
this is the karma of pride."
"I am able to speak truthfully; I am able to speak authentically; I practice according to what I have said, maintaining mindfulness and discernment"—this is the karma of pride.
"I have transcended the karma of Māra;
I have escaped the snares of the four Māras; I have severed all views; I practice patience."

Recalling and discerning these mental activities of the mind—such as these being briefly described herein—one thinks: "I have awakened to Bodhi; I have turned the Wheel of Dharma; and having caused sentient beings to attain liberation, I shall thereafter enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*."
“Recollection and conceptualization—this mental karma, O Vigour King!
All mental activities, all instances of generating the mind and engaging in speech, are entirely the karma of pride.
O Vigour King!”
What is the activity of wisdom?
In such a state, where the mind, mentation, and consciousness do not function, that is the activity of wisdom;
the bodhisattva thus constantly performs the activity of wisdom.
How does a bodhisattva constantly perform the work of wisdom?
It is said that a bodhisattva constantly performs two types of work: namely, maturing sentient beings and upholding the true Dharma.
How does a bodhisattva bring sentient beings to maturity?
It means that one brings sentient beings to maturity through the knowledge of one's own wisdom (*svajñāna*).

"Knowledge of one's own wisdom" refers to abiding in freedom from pride; thus, one knows for oneself that wherever one abides in such self-detachment, it is neither mind (*manas*) nor consciousness (*vijñāna*).
In this way, the bodhisattva is neither mind nor consciousness; thus does the bodhisattva bring sentient beings to maturity.
How does a bodhisattva embrace the true Dharma?
If a bodhisattva does not grasp at any phenomena whatsoever, this is the bodhisattva’s embracing of the true Dharma.
That which is not comprised within form is the upholding of the true Dharma;
likewise, that which is not comprised within feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness is the upholding of the true Dharma.
In this sequence, that which is not included within the elements (*dhātu*) is the upholding of the true Dharma;
that which is not included within the sense bases (*āyatana*) is the upholding of the true Dharma;
that which is neither included among wholesome dharmas nor unwholesome dharmas is the upholding of the true Dharma.

It is neither pure nor impure, neither with outflows nor without outflows, neither conditioned nor unconditioned; it is neither a mundane dharma nor a supramundane dharma—it is the gathering of the True Dharma by not being gathered in such ways.
It is the gathering of the True Dharma by not being gathered through the mark of giving, nor by morality, patience, diligence, or meditation.
Why is this? All things that arise through conditions possess the characteristic of arising; they are not the Dharma, not the Vinaya, and do not encompass the True Dharma. Why is this?
The Tathāgata’s perfect awakening is signless and unimpeded; it cannot be grasped by apprehending signs.
If a bodhisattva knows such activity, this is called wisdom;
however, if one employs this wisdom to perform the functions of wisdom, that is not the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayajñāna*).
“Vīryendrarāja! What is the ‘mastery of wisdom’ (prajñā-vaśitā)?
It refers to taking up the four kinds of unimpeded knowledge (catasraḥ pratisaṃvidaḥ) by analyzing the categories of phenomena (dharma-skandha) through phrases.”
What are the four? First, unimpededness regarding meaning; second, unimpededness regarding phenomena; third, unimpededness regarding expression; and fourth, unimpededness regarding eloquence.

"Regarding the unimpededness of meaning: among all syllables, one takes only the meaning and not the syllables—what is called 'meaning' refers to the correct knowledge of the meaning of all phenomena."

"Furthermore, 'meaning' refers to the ineffable meaning; it is the knowledge that does not forget any of the various syllables and understands their preceding and succeeding sounds—this is called 'meaning.
One attains conformity with the meaning not by grasping at words, but if one can thus maintain the equality of word and meaning, then one conforms to the meaning."
If one knows in this way, it is called "unimpededness regarding names and meanings" (*nāma-artha-pratisaṃvid*);
because there is no impediment regarding any meaning whatsoever, it is called "unimpededness regarding names and meanings.
"Unimpededness regarding phenomena" (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*) means that the phenomena are in accordance [with reality], and do not accord with what is not the Dharma.
One who accords with the Dharma does not dwell upon what is non-Dharma. Why is this?
Because all those dharmas are free from the cognition of names and words.

Regarding the unimpededness of dharmas: whether it be the vehicle or the dharma, one does not speak of them as being different from the dharma, nor does one destroy the dharma-realm within the characteristics of the dharma-realm.
Why is this? Because the dharma-realm has a single characteristic—namely, the characteristic of signlessness.
Regarding what speech does he preach? Having heard those words, their resonance is equal;

he accords with and resolves them through faith, believing that the speech of the Dharma and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) are equal. He conforms to conventional knowledge without grasping or attachment; for these reasons, it is called "unimpededness regarding phenomena" (dharmanirukti-pratisaṃvid).

"Unimpeded in expression means knowing the terminology of words—namely, the knowledge of the terminology of all beings such as nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans; the knowledge of the terminology of Śakra Devendra and Brahmā, the Lord of the World; and knowing all according to the Dharma: whether it be a single word, many words, concise words, extensive words, feminine speech, masculine speech, the speech of eunuchs, or speech of the past, future, and present."

If one uses words and speech so that other sentient beings may understand through their own minds, speaking in such a manner, then one's own words and the words of others do not obstruct one another, nor does one become attached to them.
Why is this? Because they know that all phenomena are without letters and without speech.
They reflect in this way:
"What are words and speech?
If one speaks of any phenomenon, that phenomenon does not exist within words and speech; therefore, it cannot be apprehended and cannot be expressed."
Furthermore, those syllables and words do not exist within phenomena; therefore, they cannot be apprehended and cannot be spoken.
If one speaks of syllables and words, those syllables and words possess no sound.

If these expressions—whether expressions of wholesome dharmas or expressions of unwholesome dharmas—were truly existent, they could not be apprehended; one should know that such expressions do not reside within phenomena.
One who possesses unimpeded eloquence encounters no obstruction regarding any phenomena;
thus, all phenomena do not proceed.
Why is this? Because phenomena do not proceed, all phenomena ultimately do not proceed.
Having understood it in this way, to explain it to others and to teach them so that they may understand it is called "unimpededness in terminology" (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*).
What is called "unimpededness in eloquence" (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*)?
If one is able to eloquently expound upon all speech, eloquently expound upon all sounds, and eloquently expound upon all names—
what is meant by "eloquent exposition"?
He delights in speaking of meaning, delights in speaking of the Dharma, delights in speaking of truth, and delights in speaking of reality.
If there are sentient beings who have faith and understanding in the sounds of the discourses (*sūtra*), he delights in speaking with the resonant sounds of discourses for those beings;
if they have faith and understanding in the sounds of the verses (*geya*), he then delights in speaking with the resonant sounds of verses.

In this way, whether it be *gāthā*, *geya*, *udāna*, *nidāna*, *avadāna*, *itivṛttaka*, *jātaka*, or *vaipulya* and *adbhutadharma*, he has faith and understanding in their verbal sounds; he joyfully explains them as the resonant sounds of *vaipulya* and *adbhutadharma*.
If he previously cultivated faith and understanding in their verbal sounds, he then joyfully explains them as the resonant sounds of that previous cultivation.

The eloquent discourse regarding the faculties of all sentient beings means: for those with faith, the eloquent discourse on the faculty of faith; for those with diligence, the eloquent discourse on the faculty of diligence; for those with mindfulness, the eloquent discourse on the faculty of mindfulness; for those with concentration, the eloquent discourse on the faculty of concentration; and for those with wisdom, the eloquent discourse on the faculty of wisdom. Thus, it is extensively taught that there are twenty-one thousand such eloquent discourses by Bodhisattvas concerning all the various faculties.

The Tathāgata knows eighty-four thousand faculties of those who act out of desire; the Tathāgata delights in teaching all those faculties, and the Bodhisattva, in accordance with them, delights in teaching twenty-one thousand of each of those faculties.

The Tathāgata knows eighty-four thousand faculties of those who act out of hatred; the Tathāgata delights in teaching all those faculties, and the Bodhisattva, in accordance with them, delights in teaching twenty-one thousand of each of those faculties.

The Tathāgata knows eighty-four thousand faculties of those who act out of delusion; the Tathāgata delights in teaching all those faculties, and the Bodhisattva, in accordance with them, delights in teaching twenty-one thousand of each of those faculties.

The Tathāgata knows eighty-four thousand faculties of those who practice with equanimity; the Tathāgata delights in expounding all such faculties, and the Bodhisattva, in accordance with them, delights in expounding those same eighty-four thousand faculties in twenty-one thousand ways. This is called the unimpeded eloquence of delight in expounding.

“Vīryendrarāja! Those [four] masteries—mastery over meaning, mastery over phenomena, mastery over expression, and mastery over eloquence—all such things have wisdom as their root, abide in dependence upon wisdom, and proceed in accordance with wisdom. Relying on wisdom, the bodhisattva manifests these and other various kinds of *vega* (dynamic power).”
"Furthermore, Vigourous King!
What is the root of wisdom?
Upon what does wisdom depend for its abiding?"
"How does wisdom follow along with what?
O King Vikrāntarāja!
Hearing is the root of wisdom; wisdom abides in dependence on hearing; wisdom follows along with hearing."
"Furthermore, Viravikrama!
What is the root of hearing?
Upon what does hearing depend for its abiding?"
"What does one hear as one follows whatever practice?
O King Vikrāntarāja!
A spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is the root of hearing; one who hears dwells in reliance upon the spiritual friend, and one who hears accords with the practice of the spiritual friend."
"Furthermore, Viravikrama,
what is the root of those spiritual friends?
Upon what do they abide?"
What kind of conduct does he follow?
O King Viraja!
That spiritual friend has veneration as his root; he abides in reliance upon veneration and follows veneration in his conduct.
“Furthermore, O Veṣthadhara-rāja!
What is the root of such veneration?
Upon what does it rest?”
What kind of conduct does one follow?
O King Vikrāntarāja!
Thus, profound respect has the deep mind as its root; one abides by relying on the deep mind and acts in accordance with the deep mind.
"Furthermore, O Vigourous King!
What is the root of such a profound mind?
Upon what does it abide?"
What practice does he follow?
O King Vikrānta!
Such a profound mind has non-deceit as its root; it abides in reliance upon non-deceit and follows the practice of non-deceit.
"Furthermore, Vigurāja!
What is the root of such lack of guile?
Upon what does it rely for its abiding?"
In accordance with what practice?
O King Vikrānta!
Thus, with non-deceit as its root and great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*) as its basis, one dwells in reliance upon great compassion and acts in accordance with great compassion.
"Furthermore, O Veṣthavikrāmin!
What is the root of such great compassion?
Upon what does it rely for its abiding?"
"What conduct does he follow?
O King Vikrānta!
All sentient beings are the root of great compassion; thus, he dwells in reliance upon all sentient beings and conducts himself in accordance with all sentient beings."
Why is this? O King Viraja!
It is because a bodhisattva, for the sake of bringing all sentient beings to liberation, gives rise to the mind of great compassion and omniscience.
“Vīryendrarāja! This is the vigor of wisdom;
once a bodhisattva has set forth this single Dharma-gate, whether for the duration of an eon or the remainder of an eon, they may teach various and diverse Dharmas without any obstruction.”
If he wishes to preach the Dharma for sentient beings without them seeing his body, he can do so at will;
if he wishes to cause the sound of the Dharma to issue from every pore of his own body, he can do so at will.

He expounds the Dharma with eloquence and a delight in teaching according to the deep-seated aspirations and practices of those beings; he manifests bodily forms according to those beings and expounds the Dharma, such that others who come to challenge him cannot defeat him.

"Whatever is known by the five supernatural powers of the non-Buddhists—whether it be incantations, treatises on knowledge, various discourses on Vedic wisdom, knowledge of the moon, sun, and stars, knowledge of the five elements and yin-yang, or the interpretation of dream signs; whether it be earthquakes, the *ḍākinī* mantras and various arts and techniques, or the speech of crows and other birds;
and whether it be the power of incantations that can cause deer and other animals to stop their herds from moving, or the enchantment of nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, and so forth;
or whether it be the physical characteristics of kings, deer, or other humans, or the signs of abundance and famine, or the movements and playful patterns of the stars—all such things they know."
Furthermore, he understands the various arts and skills of the world—whether writing, sealing, counting, or calculation—he understands them all;
whether it be the sounds of song, the sounds of music, the sounds of cymbals and so forth, or the rhythms, pulses, and structural points, he knows them all.
"To those such as those Brahmins and non-Buddhists, who are of all such inferior castes, one must not speak [of these things]; yet that bodhisattva has fully realized them all."
"A wise Bodhisattva is able to demonstrate all these dharmas to others, understanding them all thoroughly in this way.
Thus, the Bodhisattva skillfully knows incantations and poisons, knows the sources of incantations and poisons, and knows various treatises;
likewise, all Bodhisattvas know these things, yet they do not disturb or confuse sentient beings, nor do they believe such things to be the true path."
“Vīryendrarāja!

When a bodhisattva possesses such an exuberance of wisdom, they may sit together with ten million Brahmās, dwelling in speech, seeing one another, displaying various forms to one another, and communicating through various words to one another.”

In this way, the majestic radiance of the Bodhisattva’s various colors, such as blue and so forth, surpasses that of those Brahmās; thus, his mind has no longing for those Brahma realms, and when these Brahmās come into the presence of the Bodhisattva, they give rise to profound reverence.

Thus, while manifesting sovereign mastery within all these celestial palaces, the bodhisattva does not give rise to longing or attachment toward them, but instead gives rise to the perception of impermanence and the perception of suffering and non-self.
Bodhisattvas thus accord with the liberation of all sentient beings; O King of Agility!
This is the agility of wisdom.
O King of Agility!

Furthermore, that bodhisattva, through the power of his swift wisdom, manifests a palace within the realm of Māra—surpassing the palaces of Māra by a hundred thousandfold—causing those Māras to long for and become greedily attached to that superior palace.
Once they have given rise to such attachment, their minds become free from pride;
being thus freed from pride, he causes them to abide in *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and only thereafter does he preach the Dharma of impermanence.
"Vīryendrarāja! One should know that the conduct of a bodhisattva of wisdom is thus in all respects.
By means of this wisdom, one should know all things, whether it be giving, receiving, or making vows."
By means of this wisdom, when one protects one's own precepts and causes others to uphold the precepts, and vows to attain bodhi through this upholding of precepts—one should understand it thus.
By means of this wisdom, when one cultivates patience oneself and causes others to cultivate patience, and vows to attain bodhi through this cultivation of patience—one should understand it thus.
By means of this wisdom, when one exerts diligence oneself and causes others to exert diligence, and vows to attain bodhi through this diligence—one should understand it thus.

By means of this wisdom, whether one enters meditative absorption (*dhyāna-samāpatti*) oneself or causes others to enter meditative absorption, one should understand that through this entry into meditative absorption, one vows to attain enlightenment (*bodhi*).
By means of this wisdom, whether one gathers the teachings for oneself or explains them to others, one should understand that one observes them as they have been heard.
By means of this wisdom, one should understand all movements and comings, all modes of conduct (*īryāpatha*), and all acts of relinquishment.
“Bodhisattvas possessing wisdom, by the power of wisdom, are able to fully attain all powers of goodness;
bodhisattvas possessing wisdom, through mastery of wisdom, obtain all wealth;
bodhisattvas possessing wisdom, through the prowess of wisdom, attain supreme prowess regarding all phenomena.”
Because they grasp the power of wisdom, bodhisattvas possessing wisdom attain an adornment that resembles the adornment of a Buddha;
bodhisattvas possessing wisdom act in accordance with all phenomena without effort.
“Vīryendrarāja!
It is like when people in the world shoot an arrow upward; by exerting its own momentum, it naturally moves downward until it reaches the ground without further effort.”

Vīryaketu! It is the same for a bodhisattva endowed with wisdom: by the power of wisdom, they are able to discharge the arrow of their vows without effort, naturally falling upon the ground of all wholesome dharmas—namely, the ground of the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa)—thereby manifesting the power of wisdom.
"What further power does he possess?
By the power of wisdom, his right hand can shake as many Buddha-worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;
by the power of wisdom, he surpasses the retinues of Māra and the adornments of Māra, and even attains the ten powers of a Tathāgata encompassed within awakening."
What is power?
It is that which others cannot overcome—that which none in the entire world, including devas, humans, asuras, and so forth, can destroy.
O King Vikrāntarāja!
"This is the supernormal power of morality through the prowess of wisdom. Prowess King!
Such supernormal power of morality through the prowess of wisdom is not heard by the ears of those sentient beings who have not planted roots of goodness."
Vīryendrarāja!
If there are people who, having heard this Dharma-gate, experience joy in their hearts, such persons will be able to exercise their vigor within this very vigor.
"Why is this? Such prowess is something that none of the śrāvakas or pratyekabuddhas possess.

When the World-Honored One had finished speaking in response to the questions of the Bodhisattva Vikrāntagāmin, the Bodhisattva Vikrāntagāmin felt great joy in his heart. He joined his palms toward the Buddha, gazed at him with single-minded devotion, and without averting his eyes for a moment, spoke these words:
"All sentient beings employ these four kinds of *vikrīḍita* (mastery) as their mastery, just as the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha employs his."

At that time, the World-Honored One, before the Bodhisattva Veṣṭhita-rāja, manifested various kinds of exquisite and subtle-colored flowers, as well as flowers with leaves of various wonderful fragrances.

Then that bodhisattva took those flowers and scattered them over the Tathāgata and all the bodhisattvas in the assembly. Having thus scattered them, everything upon which the flowers landed in that assembly became adorned with golden marks, and the entire multitude saw this.
Having seen this in the midst of the sky, hundreds of thousands of devas spoke with one voice:
“World-Honored One!

If there should be anyone who has faith and understanding in such prowess, and having so believed and understood, is able to resolve upon *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, such a person adorns themselves with the adornments of the Buddha.”
Why is this? Because all such manifestations of prowess are entirely in accord with the mind of omniscience.
Furthermore, World-Honored One!
"If there are those who have not yet resolved to attain bodhicitta, where could they ever hear such inconceivable and powerful Dharma-gates as these?
At that time, the World-Honored One praised the sons of the gods in the air, saying:
"Excellent, excellent!"
Having praised him, saying "Excellent!", he addressed the Great Bodhisattva Mahāvikrāmin: "Mahāvikrāmin!
I recall that in the past, prior to the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, there was a seventh Tathāgata named Samantavimalaprabhāśrīrāja."
When that Buddha, the Tathāgata, was extensively expounding this Dharma-gate of *vikrīḍita*, there was a bodhisattva named Viṣayavat who questioned that Tathāgata regarding this Dharma-gate.

When the Tathāgata had finished expounding this Dharma-gate, eight thousand sentient beings attained this *vikrīḍita* (mastery), and furthermore, they attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Among those in the assembly, thirty-two thousand sentient beings all gave rise to the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
At that time, I attained this *vikrīḍita* (spiritual prowess), and subsequently, I fulfilled awakening under the Buddha Dīpaṃkara.
Thus it is, King Vikrīḍita!

After my parinirvāṇa, if there should be anyone who is able to hear this dharma-gate, that person, having taken up the mind set on awakening (*bodhicitta*), will certainly and swiftly attain the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
When this *vikrīḍita-dharmaparyāya* was being taught, thirty-two thousand beings among the assembly—both devas and humans—all gave rise to the mind set on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

Those devaputras rained down various kinds of flowers and offered hundreds of thousands of celestial musical instruments as an offering to the Tathāgata. Through the power of the Buddha, from within the sounds of those instruments, a wondrous voice proclaimed:

"If there are sentient beings who possess a mind of superior faith and understanding, whose faculties are sharp and keen, who have faith in and understand the Buddha-dharma, who have accomplished the practice of wisdom, who are sustained by spiritual friends, who have planted roots of goodness in past lives, and who, out of great compassion, feel pity for all sentient beings—only such persons shall hear this Dharma-gate;
having heard it, they shall believe, understand, receive, uphold, read, and recite it."
At that time, the Bodhisattva Veṣṭhitarāja addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
The Tathāgata’s ten powers, four fearlessnesses, four kinds of unimpeded knowledge, and these eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha—all such dharmas belong to the World-Honored One.”
Do Bodhisattvas possess these ten powers?
Do Bodhisattvas possess these four fearlessnesses?
Do Bodhisattvas possess these eighteen unique qualities?
The Buddha said:
"They all exist,
O Vaśavartin King!"

All Bodhisattvas, having accomplished their activities within the eighth stage, attain the ninth stage; that is to say, they possess eloquence, have attained non-retrogressive patience, and have perfected the pāramitā of skillful means and wisdom.
Vīryaketu-rāja!
When a bodhisattva is thus endowed with the ten powers and the four fearlessnesses, and accomplishes the eighteen unique dharmas, they attain the ninth stage.
“Vīryaketu, what are the ten powers of a bodhisattva?
First is the power of generating the mind of omniscience, maintaining a firm and profound resolve, fulfilling great compassion, and never abandoning any sentient beings.”
Second, the power of not seeking any material gain, offerings, or fame, and lacking the inclination to crave or delight in anything rare or extraordinary in the world;
third, the power of the ultimate Dharma, which consists of fulfilling the mind of great compassion and attaining pure faith and understanding in all Buddha-dharmas;
fourth, the power of practice through mindfulness and deportment, characterized by diligent effort without indolence and superior energy that never abandons recollection.

Fifth, the power of the immovable and abiding samādhi, which remains far removed from the two extremes and accords with the law of dependent origination, such that all views and mental activities are stilled;
sixth, the power of fulfilling the *prajñāpāramitā* because all conceptualizations, non-conceptualizations, frivolous proliferations (*prapañca*), and webs of doubt have been completely extinguished;

seventh, the power of maturing all sentient beings without ever being satiated by the immeasurable cycles of birth and death, gathering all roots of goodness in the world while regarding worldly birth and death as like a dream, and thus never growing weary within saṃsāra.

Eighth, the Bodhisattva observes that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally without sentient beings, and that its original nature is without life-force (*jīva*) or person (*pudgala*); he has faith and understanding that all phenomena are neither born nor produced, and is able to have faith and understanding in the non-arising of the wheel of phenomena, possessing the power of patience regarding the non-arising of all wheels of phenomena.

Ninth, he enters the gates of liberation through the contemplations of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, and possesses the power of the gate of liberation through the knowledge and vision of liberation in the Śrāvaka vehicle and the Pratyekabuddha vehicle.

Tenth, the Bodhisattva is able to know the profound Dharma for himself, and by observing the mental activities of all sentient beings, he possesses the power of unobstructed and perfected observation.
“Vīryaketu, these are the ten powers of a bodhisattva. Vīryaketu!”

What are the four fearlessnesses of a bodhisattva? First, the bodhisattva retains everything they hear, attains dhāraṇī, and remembers it without forgetting; thus, they fearlessly preach the Dharma to the great assembly.

Second, the bodhisattva has faith and understanding in all phenomena and thereby attains the power of patience (*kṣānti*); having realized that phenomena are neither born nor produced, they attain the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Having attained this patience regarding phenomena, they enter into the dharmas of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness; thus, they fearlessly preach the Dharma to the great assembly.

Third, the Bodhisattva contemplates the gates of liberation in the Śrāvaka vehicle and understands the faith, knowledge, and vision of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle; he has faith in all the bases of totality (*kṛtsnāyatana*) and also faith in liberation. Just as one knows the medicines required for the various illnesses of sentient beings, so too does he know the ripening of the faculties of all sentient beings, and likewise knows how to preach the Dharma accordingly. In this way, the Bodhisattva fearlessly preaches the Dharma to the great assembly.

Fourth, the Bodhisattva is free from the fear of the great assembly. At that time, he has no such thought: "If someone comes from the east, west, south, or north to challenge me with questions and I cannot answer, I shall be afraid and unable to respond. He perceives no sign of fear. Thus, when any sentient being questions or challenges him, the Bodhisattva is able to answer them all. In accordance with their inquiries, he provides explanations and answers without any dread, capable of severing all doubts in sentient beings and preaching the Dharma without fearing the great assembly.
"Vīryaketu, these are the four fearlessnesses of a bodhisattva. Vīryaketu!"
What are the eighteen unique qualities of a bodhisattva? O King Vikrāntarāja! They are as follows:

a bodhisattva practices giving by relinquishing wealth and possessions even without being taught by anyone; furthermore, from the very moment of birth, they are able to conceive the intention to give away their wealth in charity.
Furthermore, if the Māra King assumes the form of a Buddha and says such words as,
"If a person practices giving, they will enter hell," that Bodhisattva does not give rise to stinginess or envy.

Furthermore, a bodhisattva gives away all his own possessions; his mind of giving becomes increasingly superior. Such giving is the cause of bodhi; he does not hope for karmic retribution, but vows to dedicate it all to all sentient beings.
Vīryavega-rāja!
This is the first unique quality of a bodhisattva.
Vīryavega-rāja!

Furthermore, even without being taught by anyone—and while that bodhisattva has no place to receive the precepts because a Tathāgata has not yet appeared—they aspire to train in the correct practice of the *prātimokṣa*, never abandoning this uncommon quality.

When a bodhisattva lives at home, they protect the precepts as taught; although they have not gone forth and have no teacher, they train according to what is explained in the *Prātimokṣa*. Even for the sake of saving their life, they do not abandon the training in the precepts. All training in the precepts accords with awakening, and they vow to sever the breaking of precepts among all sentient beings.
"Vikrāntarāja!
This is the second unique quality of a bodhisattva. Vikrāntarāja!"
Furthermore, when all sentient beings revile, insult, or mutilate his body, a bodhisattva does not give rise to a mind of anger.

Whether it be a poor person, an outcaste (*caṇḍāla*), a *pukkaśa*, or a craftsman who insults and humbles him in various ways, the bodhisattva’s mind likewise does not give rise to anger; he universally covers those sentient beings with a heart of loving-kindness, and though they possess great power to inflict evil upon him, he does not commit evil in return.
In this way, the bodhisattva acts in accordance with the Dharma;
in this way, sentient beings are the very causes and conditions for the Buddha-dharma of the bodhisattva;
and in this way, the bodhisattva brings peace to the minds of those sentient beings and provides them benefit, donning the armor of patience and rousing heroic strength.
"Vīryendrarāja!
This is the third unique quality of a bodhisattva. Vīryendrarāja!"
Furthermore, even if a bodhisattva encounters many forms of decline and affliction, they diligently practice *dhūta* austerities without abandoning them or giving rise to a spirit of inferiority.
Seeing the śrāvaka vehicle enter into nirvāṇa and perceiving the suffering of saṃsāra, their mind does not seek the nirvāṇa of the śrāvaka;
seeing the pratyekabuddha vehicle enter into nirvāṇa and perceiving the suffering of saṃsāra, their mind likewise does not seek the nirvāṇa of the pratyekabuddha.

Seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One Sarvārthasiddha, having accomplished all the qualities of a Buddha and completed what was to be done, entering into parinirvāṇa; and knowing for himself that he did not yet possess such power while sentient beings had not yet fulfilled the Buddha-dharmas, his mind did not become discouraged. He gave rise to a mind of diligence, thinking:
"I, too, shall enter parinirvāṇa just as the Buddha has."
"Vikrāntarāja! This is the fourth unique quality of a bodhisattva. Vikrāntarāja!"

Furthermore, whether as a wheel-turning monarch, a king of the Śakras, or a lord of Māras surrounded by women, and though possessing divine songs and music and every kind of exquisite pleasure, the Bodhisattva enters meditative absorption therein and cultivates the immeasurables; yet his mind delights in the dharma of detachment from desire and does not follow divergent speech.

He feels great terror toward birth and death; he conceives the perception of impurity regarding the dharma of sensual desire; he conceives the perception of an enemy toward the aggregates (*skandha*); he conceives the perception of a venomous snake toward the elements (*dhātu*); he conceives the perception of an empty village toward the sense bases (*āyatana*); he conceives the perception of death toward his own kinsmen; and he conceives the perception of a cemetery toward women.

Their minds always delight in seeking to embrace the True Dharma; they long to see the Buddhas and draw near to make offerings to them; they also never disparage any sentient beings, and are able to cause the sounds of meditative factors to emerge from musical instruments, stringed songs, and the like.

Once Māra had heard this, his obstruction caused the sound to vanish; however, by the power of that bodhisattva’s prior roots of goodness, the sounds of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha immediately emerged from the midst of the sky.
Furthermore, that bodhisattva renounces his kingdom, wealth, pleasures, and sovereignty, and enters the mountain forests.
O Vikrāntarāja!
This is the fifth unique quality of a bodhisattva.

“Vīryaketu, furthermore, within all the meditative concentrations of the world, a bodhisattva does not give rise to the notion of solidity; they possess wise conduct, remain far removed from latent tendencies and views, and grasp at meaning and the Dharma.
In this way, even in dreams, such a bodhisattva does not give rise to the view of self, does not give rise to the view of others, and does not give rise to the view of dharmas.”
Regarding these unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*): if one has self-view, then there will be underlying tendencies toward views; because one lacks self-view, one is free from the net of doubt.
Māra Pāpīyān cannot cause such a person to give rise to views based on doubt; for if one has views based on doubt, one is alienated from the Dharma.
In this way, the bodhisattva brings sentient beings to maturity and benefits them, disregarding his own delusions and remaining free from doubt.
O King Vikrāntarāja,
this is the sixth unique quality of a bodhisattva.

“Vīryendrarāja! Furthermore, the bodhisattva, being free from all birth and without effortful exertion, has pure physical action (*kāyakarman*). He is far removed from taking life and bestows fearlessness upon all sentient beings. Whether with his hand, a clod of earth, a staff, or a sword, he does not inflict harm upon sentient beings; he remains far removed from weapons and staves, and does not grasp them in his hands.”
One is content with one's own wealth; regarding the possessions of others, one neither takes nor accepts even as much as a single handful of grass.
Even if the earth were filled with jewels, one would not give rise to a greedy mind. One would rather lose body and life than ever take wealth, clothing, or food through wrong livelihood.
One constantly practices the holy life (*brahmacarya*), never giving rise to thoughts of sensual desire or gluttony.

In this way, the bodhisattva remains free from desire, strife, and all afflictions, and does not engage in unwholesome dharmas caused by sexual desire; having first reflected upon this, that bodhisattva accomplishes physical action as a unique quality of his own.
Vīryaketu! This is the seventh unique quality of a bodhisattva. Vīryaketu!

Furthermore, the Bodhisattva purifies his verbal karma by speaking truthfully and speaking authentically; he acts according to what he says, and does not deceive the Tathāgatas, devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, humans, or non-humans.

One does not utter evil speech; one does not cause the breaking up of one's retinue, but cherishes one's own followers. One avoids harsh speech, speaking instead with words of love, gentle words, and not with coarse or rugged words. One speaks appropriately, speaks for the benefit of others, and always initiates conversation with a smiling countenance.

In this way, the bodhisattva refrains from all harsh speech, abusive speech, words that others find unpleasant, and words that cause distress to oneself or others; he does not speak words that contradict his mind—saying "no" when there is nothing, and saying "yes" when there is something. Through such pure speech and deep-seated pure faith, he attains the uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*) of always obtaining, in every place of birth, speech that accords with the Dharma and is consistent with the Dharma.
By such speech, they are able to cause the minds of all those with impure thoughts to attain purity; those whose minds are pure are then able to make offerings.

Because of their profound mind and its unique qualities, they always obtain truthful speech; whatever they say is not different from the words themselves, and everything they utter is exactly as it is.
Vīryavega-rāja!
This is the eighth unique quality of a bodhisattva.
Vīryavega-rāja!
Furthermore, the Bodhisattva possesses mastery over his own mind; he is without greed, without anger, and possesses right view rather than wrong view.

Thus, the Bodhisattva’s bodhicitta is a mind without equal; it is neither forgotten nor lost, and it remains far removed from all deceitful minds, crooked minds, turbid minds, and distracted minds, constantly practicing pure compassion day and night.
Vīryaketu! This is the ninth unique quality of a bodhisattva. Vīryaketu!

Furthermore, at the very moment of his birth, the Bodhisattva was endowed with worldly knowledge; whether it be incantations, recitations, medicine, pharmacology, calligraphy, seals, mathematics, or calculation, he knew them all. He possessed immediate and manifest knowledge of all teachers' arts, was well-versed in all skills and treatises, and regarding both mundane and supramundane dharmas, he did not rely on others for knowledge. Having accomplished this through his own wisdom, he did not look to the faces of others.
When all devas and humans observe the Bodhisattva, they have this thought:
"If the Bodhisattva speaks, we shall listen and practice accordingly.
O King Vikrānta!
This is the tenth unique quality of a bodhisattva. "Vikrāntarāja!

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva benefits sentient beings through various means, he is able to treat the illnesses and ailments of others without seeking wealth, profit, offerings, or fame. With great compassion as his primary motive, he heals the world and subsequently establishes them in supramundane dharmas."
Thus, the Bodhisattva constantly reflects in his mind:

"By what skillful means, at what time, and by what teaching can these sentient beings in this evil world of suffering and affliction be liberated? Having been liberated, how may they ultimately sever all afflictions—that is, eliminate all suffering and distress—and cause them to abide in the ultimate bliss of Nirvana?"
“Vīryaketu, this is the eleventh unique quality of a bodhisattva. Vīryaketu!”

Furthermore, the bodhisattva’s mind harbors no aspiration or vow for the position of Śakra Devendra, or Brahmā Devendra, or a universal monarch (cakravartin) ruling over a kingdom, yet these are nonetheless attained.

In this way, although that bodhisattva does not seek the station of Śakra Devendra, the realm of Brahmā, or the status of a holy universal monarch ruling over a kingdom, they are spontaneously obtained despite the absence of such longing.

Furthermore, that bodhisattva does not seek the holy life for the sake of form; he does not seek physical beauty, nor a kingdom, nor retinues, nor wealth, nor fame, nor the marks of physical excellence. Thus, although he does not hope for them, he attains the fulfillment of this holy life.
Vīryaketu! This is the twelfth unique quality of a bodhisattva. Vīryaketu!

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva dwells in a favorable land and a place of wealth and happiness yet does not know how to recollect the Buddha, there are devas who have previously seen the Buddha and instruct them to do so. Having first rebuked them, they teach them thus:
"This dharma should be practiced; this should not be practiced. If you perform these deeds, you shall attain bodhi; you should make such a vow."
"By acting and practicing in this way, you shall subdue your sense faculties and, in the future, attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Thus that deva instructed him, causing him to remain mindful of the path to enlightenment, neither transgressing nor abandoning it.
Vīryaketu! This is the thirteenth unique quality of a bodhisattva. Vīryaketu!

Furthermore, as for what kind of evil persons—beings with many evils, much anger, and defiled minds—the Bodhisattva cannot be harmed by them, nor does the Bodhisattva retaliate against them with evil.
Even those who are great evildoers and full of anger—whether their body, speech, or mind is wicked—will have their minds immediately become pure upon seeing a bodhisattva.
Why is this? Because the bodhisattva does not retaliate against their evil; rather, they establish those evildoers within the true Dharma to purify their minds.
Although they commit evil, by the power of the bodhisattva, they do not enter the evil realms.
Why is this? Because that bodhisattva, from the very beginning, has fulfilled the purity of these uncommon precepts and possesses such a thought:
"If there are sentient beings who, through bodily action, verbal action, or mental action, give rise to ill will toward me, may those sentient beings not fall into the evil realms."
"Because they possess the precepts, their vows are accomplished accordingly.
O Virasena! This is the fourteenth unique quality of a bodhisattva."
"Vīryaketu, furthermore,

if there are sentient beings who lack faith— being stingy, greedy, holding wrong views, and indolent— who do not believe in the retribution of karma, and who are alienated from the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha."

If, toward a śramaṇa or a brāhmaṇa, one’s mind is not pure, then one does not pay homage upon seeing them; nor does one make offerings, nor give rise to reverence, nor even give rise to a sense of wonder.

When such sentient beings see a bodhisattva, they immediately abide in dignified deportment; when they hear his speech, their minds become pure, and they rise to welcome him, prostrate, make offerings, show respect, and give rise to a sense of wonder.
Why is this? It is because of the power of that bodhisattva,
O King Vaśavartin!
This is the fifteenth unique quality of a bodhisattva. "Vikrāntarāja!

Furthermore, if there are devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, ṛṣis, or brahmins who conceive the thought of the bodhisattva as their teacher, those who are the foremost teachers among all the worlds shall all take the bodhisattva as their teacher."
By means of his supernormal powers, he is able to cause the world’s devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, ṛṣis, and brahmins to all come and pay him homage.
Once they have arrived, they follow the Bodhisattva’s words, prostrating to the Bodhisattva, making offerings, and showing him respect; these beings all first take him as their leader.
Upon seeing the Bodhisattva, they immediately prostrate, revere, and honor him, conceiving thoughts of his supreme excellence and developing deep faith and respect.
O Viravikrāmin!
This is the sixteenth unique quality of a bodhisattva.
O Viravikrāmin!

Furthermore, wherever a bodhisattva is born and into whatever lineage—whether in a village, a city, or a place where people gather—there the wholesome dharmas of sentient beings increase, unwholesome dharmas are severed, and he brings sentient beings to maturity while gathering them into the true Dharma.

Born into a family of right view, with parents of right faith, right conduct, and right entry, wherever in whatever region among human beings a Bodhisattva is born, he is the most excellent among teachers; there, the multitude offers him offerings and respect, and not a single sentient being enters the evil realms.
Just as those beings are embraced by the roots of goodness of that bodhisattva, when they die in that place, they are reborn in the heavens or among human beings.
O Vigraharāja, this is the seventeenth unique quality of a bodhisattva.
“Vīryendrarāja!

Furthermore, when a bodhisattva accords with all factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma) and fulfills the supreme supernormal powers (abhijñā), no māras can find an opportunity to gain advantage over them.”
Vīryaketu! This is the eighteenth unique quality of a bodhisattva. Vīryaketu!
"Regarding the 'unshared dharmas' (āveṇika-dharma), why are they called unshared?
Because all Buddha-dharmas accord with right practice, they are named unshared dharmas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Vegeśvara addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
How rare!
World-Honored One!”
The Tathāgata is indeed able to bestow the great light of the Dharma upon all bodhisattvas and to produce immeasurable, supreme radiance.
As I understand the meaning of the Dharma taught by the Buddha:
if there is a bodhisattva who hears this Dharma-gate and, upon it once reaching their ears, attains a pure mind, other sūtras cannot achieve such a result.
If, having heard it, one receives, maintains, reads, and recites it, that person then encompasses all Buddha-dharmas;

if a person can correctly contemplate this Dharma-gate, they have already cultivated all Buddha-dharmas and will attain the conforming patience (*ānulomikī kṣānti*) regarding all dharmas within this Dharma-gate;
if there are those who can practice this Dharma-gate, all Buddha-dharmas have already been practiced by them.
It should be understood in this way.
Furthermore, World-Honored One,
if a person does not depart from this Dharma-gate, they will attain supernormal powers.
"In this way, once a bodhisattva has attained the supernormal powers, they shall abide at the site of enlightenment.
The Buddha said, "So it is, so it is."
Vīryaketu! As you have said, if a person does not depart from this dharma-gate, they shall attain supernormal powers;
likewise, once a bodhisattva has attained these powers, they shall abide at the site of enlightenment.

“Vikrāntarāja! Long ago, in a past age even further back than before the time of the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara, there was a Buddha named Padmaprabha. Even further back than that, there was another Tathāgata named Tiṣya. Even further back than that, there was another Tathāgata named Puṣya. Even further back than that, there was another Tathāgata named Bhadra. Even further back than that, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata, Arhat, and World-Honored One named Devendra.”
"At that time, in the world-system of that Tathāgata, the Heavenly King Buddha, all things were fully provided for; it was peaceful, prosperous, and joyful, and the devas and humans flourished."
The ground is as level as the palm of a hand, interspersed with various kinds of *vaiḍūrya*, Jāmbūnada gold, and *padma* flowers;
the earth is soft and supple, its texture like that of *kācalindika* cloth.

The people enjoy peace and happiness like those in Tuṣita; whatever food and drink they require arrives swiftly according to their thoughts. Their physical complexions, features, places of recreation, and various palaces are no different from those of the devas; the only distinction is that the two names, "deva" and "human," differ.
“Within this trichiliocosm there is no other king; there is only the Tathāgata, and for this reason he is called the Heavenly King (*devendra*).

Just as a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*) sits upon the throne of benefit and governs the world according to the Dharma rather than what is not the Dharma, so too is the Tathāgata, the Heavenly King:
seated upon the lion throne of the Dharma seat, he teaches the Dharma to the devas and humans as is appropriate.”

When he wished to preach the Dharma, a great assembly filled the eight thousand four hundred yojanas of space extending east, west, south, and north; at that time, the Tathāgata’s voice of the Dharma pervaded the three thousandfold world system.

Those devas and humans make offerings to, revere, prostrate before, and honor the Tathāgata, performing what is known as the unsurpassed offering of the Buddha-dharma; they are beings whose faith and understanding are not inferior, for they believe solely in the Buddha-dharma.
Thus, in that place, even the names of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas do not exist;
how could there be any vehicle, much less any practice?
There were only a pure assembly of great bodhisattvas surrounding the World-Honored One.
That place is pure and free of women; from the very beginning, the name of sensual desire has never been heard there.
All those sentient beings are born by transformation, sitting cross-legged within lotus flowers.
Thus, those humans and devas born by transformation experience three kinds of bliss.
What are the three? They are:
the bliss of beholding the Tathāgata, the bliss of hearing the Dharma, and the bliss of observing the True Dharma and becoming free from desire.
Those devas and humans are not heedless; they possess abundant wealth, preach the Dharma to one another, and are constantly diligent and energetic.
Their lifespans are long, immeasurable, and incalculable; when their karma is exhausted and they pass away, they are not reborn in other realms, but are born in Buddha-worlds.
"In this way, when a bodhisattva is about to descend, they ascend into the air to a height of seven tala trees and utter these words:
'I now descend from this buddha-world.'"

Upon hearing that voice, immeasurable bodhisattvas all gathered together in harmony and assembled; observing that bodhisattva manifesting the patience of dharmas (dharmakṣānti), they spoke these words:
"From what dharma has he regressed?"
"In what dharma do they arise?
Then that regressing bodhisattva spoke these words within that assembly of bodhisattvas:
"Great Seer, you should know:
There is not the slightest dharma that either declines or arises;
all dharmas realized by the Tathāgata are entirely without decline and entirely without arising.
It is not that form declines, nor is it that form arises.
There is no falling away or arising in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness.

Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no self (*ātman*) and no life-principle (*jīva*); nor is there any sentient being (*sattva*), person (*pudgala*), human, or non-human who falls away or arises.

The World-Honored One has perfectly awakened to the fact that all phenomena are empty, signless, and wishless; within these phenomena of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, there is neither falling back nor arising.

The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, has realized the limit of freedom from desire, realized the limit of the unconditioned, and realized the limit of non-arising. Within the limit of non-arising, there is no falling back and no arising; because there are no causes or conditions for falling back, he does not fall back.
"Because the causes and conditions for non-arising do not harmonize, there is no arising.
Thus, these causes and conditions neither harmonize, nor do they cease, nor do they arise.
Having thus taught this Dharma to the assembly of bodhisattvas, the Bodhisattva then withdrew.
When those regressing bodhisattvas have thus regressed, they are without body, without skin, without mass, and without anything that can be known or seen;
having regressed, they again reach other buddha-worlds where they manifest before the Tathāgatas.
“The Tathāgata Devarāja and his bodhisattvas do not wear the kashaya robes, but all wear pure and exquisite celestial garments.

Without training in the precepts, they are all perfectly disciplined; having all attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), he does not extensively preach the Dharma for the assembly of bodhisattvas.”
Why is this? Because all those in that assembly have little learning yet possess great understanding due to their sharp faculties.
When that Tathāgata preaches the Dharma for the assembly of bodhisattvas, once he has finished preaching, everyone—whether humans or devas—everywhere, even throughout that Buddha-world, knows it all.

Among those various sentient beings, some attained patience (*kṣānti*), some obtained dhāraṇīs, some attained eloquence (*pratibhāna*), and some attained samādhi; at that time, the fame of that Tathāgata spread throughout the ten directions.

“Vīryaketu! The Tathāgata Devendra extensively expounded and analyzed this Dharma-gate for the sake of devas and humans, and seventy-two thousand bodhisattvas all received their predictions of enlightenment.”
In that assembly there was a bodhisattva named Vimalaviśuddhaprabha who had not yet received a prediction of enlightenment. He thought to himself:

"The deportment, mindfulness, mental conduct, wisdom, supernormal powers, attainment of dhāraṇīs, and attainment of samādhis of these bodhisattvas are no superior to mine, yet they have all received predictions."
"If they have received their prediction, for what reason have I not been granted one?
When the Tathāgata Heavenly King knew what that bodhisattva was thinking in his heart, he said to him:
"In a future age, you shall receive your prediction."
“Good son!
In a future age, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha Dīpaṃkara shall bestow upon you the prediction of enlightenment.
When the Bodhisattva Vimalaviśuddhaprabha heard these words, his heart was filled with joy; he ascended into the air and spoke these words:
"If, in a future age as vast as the sands of the Ganges, the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara appears in the world, may I attain all-knowledge at that time;
for the Tathāgata speaks truth, the Tathāgata speaks reality, and his words do not differ from the fact."
"Vīryaketu, what do you think?
Was that Great Bodhisattva Vimalaprabha at that time anyone other than yourself?"
Do not view this otherwise. Why is that?
I was the Bodhisattva Vimalaprabhā at that time.
“Vikrāntarāja! Subsequently, there was a Tathāgata named Pācīna; at that time, I made offerings to that Buddha, and that Buddha expounded this Dharma-gate for me.”
Having heard this, I received, upheld, recited, and chanted it; at that time, I attained the Samādhi of the Seal of Light.

Subsequently, there was a Tathāgata named Puṣya; at that time, I made offerings to that Buddha, heard this Dharma-gate, received, upheld, recited, and chanted it, and at that time, I attained the Samādhi of Radiance.
"Subsequently, he made offerings to the Tathāgata Tiṣya, heard this Dharma-gate, received and upheld it, recited and chanted it, and further attained the Vairocana-samādhi."

"Subsequently, he made offerings to the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, Padmaprabha; having heard this Dharma-gate, he received, upheld, read, and recited it, thereby attaining the patience of compliance (anulomikī-kṣānti)."

"Afterward, I made offerings to the Tathāgata Dīpaṃkara; at that time, I attained the patience regarding the non-arising of phenomena (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti). I then attained these four kinds of prowess (vikrīḍita)—namely, the prowess of ethical discipline (śīla), the prowess of supernormal powers (abhijñā), the prowess of knowledge (jñāna), and the prowess of wisdom (prajñā)."
“Vīryendrarāja! This gate is thus; you should understand it well.

If there is anyone—whether a son of good family or a daughter of good family—who practices the bodhisattva path and now hears, receives, upholds, reads, and recites this Dharma-gate from me, they shall all swiftly attain the supernormal powers and achieve this *vīrya* (mastery).”
"Having attained such vigor, they shall turn the great wheel of Dharma and obtain the light of wisdom within this unsurpassed Dharma of Radiance.

When the Tathāgata spoke this Dharma-gate, sixteen thousand bodhisattvas in the assembly all attained patience (*kṣānti*), and furthermore, twelve thousand sentient beings gave rise to the mind of enlightenment (*bodhicitta*).
The trichiliocosm shook, and hundreds of thousands of devas all uttered words of praise, saying:
"Wherever this Dharma-gate resides, there is a Buddha; only those sentient beings who have deeply planted roots of goodness are able to hear such a Dharma-gate."
At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
by what name should this Dharma-gate be called?”
"How should this Dharma-gate be received and upheld?
The Buddha said, "Ānanda!"
"This dharma-gate is named 'The Dharma-Gate of the Four Vaipulya Superknowledges'; it should be upheld in this way.

When the World-Honored One had finished speaking, the Bodhisattva Vaipulyarāja, the Venerable Ānanda, along with all the devas, humans, gandharvas, asuras, and others, having heard what the Tathāgata said, rejoiced and praised him.
The Sūtra of the Questions of the King Vighuṣṭarāja, Scroll II.
